title: Indonesian Zombie Franchise ‘Zona Merah: Dead City’ Unveils Teaser, Takes Outbreak Into the City
full_text: Oct 16, 2026 6:41am PT Indonesian Zombie Franchise ‘Zona Merah: Dead City’ Unveils Teaser, Takes Outbreak Into the City By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Boo Junfeng’s ‘Trinity,’ Sidharta Tata’s ‘Slaughterground’ Among JAFF Market 2026 Selections 2 hours ago Singapore Media Festival Launches Creator Summit as Asia TV Forum Adds AI Zone, Microdrama Focus 5 hours ago Busan Takeaways: Record Crowds Meet a Political Storm as Asia’s Producers Close Ranks 6 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Screenplay Films The first teaser for “ Zona Merah : Dead City,” the big-screen adaptation of Indonesian zombie series “Zona Merah,” has landed ahead of the film’s Jan. 14, 2027, release in Indonesian cinemas. Screenplay Films, which unveiled the trailer on Friday, is billing the feature as the largest zombie production Indonesia has ever mounted. The source series, a Vidio original, has racked up more than 34 million views on the streamer. The film follows survivors struggling to outlast an undead threat that grows far beyond anything the show attempted. title: Rafe Spall On Playing An Amnesiac Super Sleuth In ‘The Death Of Sherlock Holmes’: “This Is A Clean Slate”
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Hudson Williams, Zach Galifianakis & Jay Baruchel Set For ‘The Assembly’ Season 2 At Canada’s CBC ‘Down Cemetery Road’: Apple TV Detective Drama Adds 12 To Season 2 Radial Entertainment Completes Busy MIPCOM Week With ‘Making A Serial Killer’ Season 3 Order View All October 16, 2026 6:37am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'The Death of Sherlock Holmes' Fabienne Berchtold, Silver Reel Rafe Spall was one of the biggest names at MIPCOM Cannes this week where he gave Deadline his take on playing super sleuth Sherlock Holmes. The Trying star is leading The Death of Sherlock Holmes , which fills the gap between the detective’s apparent death at the Reichenbach Falls in 1891 and his reappearance in The Adventure of the Empty House three years later. Set against the Swiss Alps, the story follows an Englishman (Spall) found barely alive in an icy mountain stream by local woman Alma ( Deleila Piasko ) and her young son, Franz. When the village doctor is found murdered, villagers turn on the boy – leaving the amnesiac stranger, who is experiencing flashbacks to a previous life in England, as his only hope as his powers of deduction return. Related Stories News International Insider: Surfing To MIPCOM Cannes; Russell Brand Trial Begins; Nicole Wallace Interview Executives BBC Studios' Boss Says Streaming Is The Future But Linear Still Pays The Bills “What makes it original is the fact that he’s someone who has no idea who he is,” Spall told us at the Majestic Hotel on the Croisette. “He gets these flashes of brilliant deduction that lead him toward understanding what kind of person he is, and eventually perhaps figuring out that he’s the most famous detective in the world.” Watch on Deadline Piasko said the relationship between Holmes and Alma is central to the story. “What’s very special is that this Englishman doesn’t judge her,” she added. “She’s a single mother living in a small village, and she’s treated with contempt, experiencing a kind of exclusion. With him, it’s different.” Spall said these circumstances of amnesia allowed him to create a fresh take on the character and freed him from comparison to other Sherlocks. “It’s a clean slate in a way. I didn’t feel like I was following in a long line of great actors who have played him in the past — Benedict Cumberbatch, Jeremy Brett, Basil Rathbone, Robert Downey Jr. and all these amazing people.” The show is a co-production between Sky and SRF in Switzerland, Germany’s ARD Degeto and the Bell Media-owned Sphere Abacus, which brought Spall to Cannes this week. The series will broadcast on Sky in the U.K. and Ireland and also goes out on Sky in Switzerland and Germany. FFF Bayern from Germany and Italy’s IDM Film Commission are supporting the series. Spall’s face was all over town given he’s also starring in Channel 4 drama Number 10 , which ITV Studios has been shopping. He talked about playing a British Prime Minister – revealing he actually met one in the research phase – and addressed his role as Arthur Weasley in the upcoming HBO TV series Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone – chuckling as he compared his role with that of his dad, Timothy Spall, in the movie series. Here’s the full interview with Spall and Piasko. DEADLINE: Rafe, There are lots of different versions of Sherlock coming through at any one time. This one is slightly unique in that he is suffering from amnesia and doesn’t know who he is. How did that color what you wanted to bring to the character? What did you think was the core of this version of Sherlock? RAFE SPALL: What makes it original is the fact that he’s someone who has no idea who he is. He gets these flashes of brilliant deduction that lead him toward understanding what kind of person he is, and eventually perhaps figuring out that he’s the most famous detective in the world. It’s a clean slate in a way. I didn’t feel like I was following in a long line of great actors who have played him in the past — Benedict Cumberbatch, Jeremy Brett, Basil Rathbone, Robert Downey Jr. and all these amazing people. The comparison is somewhat taken away by the fact that I can say, if people think I’m rubbish in it, that it’s a different Sherlock Holmes. It was completely different. I would have been much more frightened if it had been one of the Conan Doyle novels, which is what Steven Moffat adapted. But the great characters in the modern Western canon are always ripe for interpretation. Hamlet gets done every year, and so does Sherlock Holmes, because they’re great pieces of work and great characters that can sustain different shapes and approaches. DEADLINE: Deleila, when Sherlock — or whoever he is at the start of the show — comes into Alma’s life, what does she make of this man who seems to have come from nowhere? He could be helpful, or he could be a disaster for her. DELEILA PIASKO: They are strangers, and they become partners in crime. We tell the story of them getting to know each other. They are both lost in the world, so their relationship is really at the core of the show. It’s about the relationship between the Englishman and Alma. It’s a journey with them. Alma realizes that she needs him. She’s a lone wolf, but at one point she needs a partner — somebody to help her. What’s very special is that this Englishman doesn’t judge her. She’s a single mother living in a small village, and she’s treated with contempt. She’s experiencing a kind of exclusion. With him, it’s different. It’s the beginning of a friendship — or whatever it becomes. DEADLINE: Most Sherlock Holmes stories are mysteries – intricate, complex and brilliantly written. Would you describe this series as a mystery, or does it fit somewhere else tonally? SPALL: Fans of the genre will be satisfied by the whodunit – the question of how something happened and the mysterious nature of it. They’ll also get a thrill from seeing flashes of this famous character’s powers of deduction. What’s interesting is that Conan Doyle got sick of writing Sherlock Holmes. He killed him off, with Holmes and Moriarty falling off the Reichenbach Falls. Then, I think, he missed the money, so three years later he brought him back. This is the first attempt I can think of to fill in the gap of what happened, so it isn’t based on a Conan Doyle novel. It’s a new story that, hopefully, fulfils people’s expectations of a Sherlock Holmes story. There’s a lot of mystery and a classic Holmes whodunit at its heart. DEADLINE: When did you first hear about the project, and what drew you to it? SPALL: My agent called and said they were doing a new version of Sherlock Holmes and asked if I’d like to speak to the people making it. I found it very charming and nice, and I thought it was really original. I was asked, I said yes, and here we are. It was probably about a year ago that it came to me, although I think the project had been around for a while and was then pulled together quite rapidly. DEADLINE: Deleila, was it a similar process for you? PIASKO: Yes, pretty much the same time. I read the script and thought it was fantastic. I was very lucky. SPALL: We had a fun time because we were filming in some pretty rough-and-ready places — the Swiss Alps, the Italian Alps and a great town called Regensburg in Bavaria. We were in fairly remote locations, so it was very important to be surrounded by nice people. We really got on with each other and had a good time making it. DEADLINE: With European co-productions, different parties can sometimes pull in different directions to serve their respective audiences. Did this feel more holistic and complete? PIASKO: There were many different approaches. Our show is about cultural clashes, and of course there are different experiences. It’s also a multilingual show, so behind the scenes you have to communicate somehow, but I think that’s the beauty of it. It makes the world bigger and fleshes it out, especially when you have different languages. It was very free creatively. We were very welcome to bring our nerves and our ideas into it. SPALL: From a trade point of view, it’s an interesting example of a new way of putting together big television in Europe. The bottom has fallen out of the American co-production market and a new way needed to be found. I can only speak from an English point of view, or as someone who predominantly makes British film and television, but I think there have been some very successful examples of this new model. This series is an example of the way the industry has changed and evolved. When it came to me, I knew Sky Switzerland and Sky Germany were putting up the initial money, and it was then acquired by Sky UK, which I had previously worked with. I was the only English person involved, which felt appropriate because Sherlock Holmes is in the Swiss Alps. DEADLINE: Rafe, you’re doing a lot of work at the moment. What does the next year or two look like for you? SPALL: I’m doing Harry Potter at the moment. If people like it, I’ll be doing that for a long time. Then I’m going to do Under Salt Marsh Season 2 next year. I’ve got Number 10 , which I think is coming soon, and ITV Studios is selling that. Maybe there’ll be another season of Trying — we’ll see. Who knows? I’m very lucky to be paid to do a job I love. It’s the only skill I could possibly exchange for cash. No one else would accept money for anything else I could offer. DEADLINE: And what does the next couple of years look like for you, Deleila? PIASKO: There are some things in the pipeline, but I can’t share them yet. Maybe there will be in a second season of The Death of Sherlock Holmes — we’ll see. There are also some other projects, including the German TV show Zweifel , which won Best Series at the Cannes Series festival in 2024. The second season will air next January. DEADLINE: Are you nervous about Harry Potter , Rafe? We’re hearing the sets are looking amazing, like nothing else. SPALL: I’ve never seen production values like it. I’ve been lucky enough to do things such as Prometheus and Jurassic World , big franchise projects, but I’ve never seen sets like these. Kate Hall, who does the hair and make up and worked on The Crown , is extraordinary. Holly Waddington, who won an Oscar for Poor Things , is doing the costumes. I’ve never come out of costume fittings feeling so excited. I was around true genius — a costume designer who just blows my mind. So I’m not nervous about it. I’m just really enjoying it. It’s funny that my dad played Ron’s rat and now I’m playing Arthur Weasley. The other day I was on set and Ron’s rat was there. I took a photograph next to it. If I had social media, I would post it. DEADLINE: Talking of which, do you worry about the social media reaction, given the controversy surrounding J.K. Rowling? SPALL: I’m mercifully not on any form of social media, and I don’t feel I have anything further to contribute to that debate. I’m just feeling really lucky to be part of something full of amazingly creative, brilliant people, all working at the top of their game. There are fabulous actors involved. Katherine Parkinson and I play the Weasley parents, and to my mind, she’s one of the best actors in the world. She’s phenomenal. The other day it was me, her, Kit Harington and Johnny Flynn. It was just fun. DEADLINE: You’ve said you’re hoping for a second season of The Death of Sherlock Holmes … SPALL: If people like it, we’ll do more of it. There are more stories to tell. WHITTOCK: I also wanted to ask you about Number 10 . The British prime minister is obviously never just one person and can be whoever you want him to be. But there is a picture in people’s minds of what the prime minister is. What was your take on playing that character? SPALL: It was pretty thrilling. It was one of the most challenging things I’ve ever done because Steven Moffat writes 10-page scenes, which is rare in modern television. And for a writer of Stephen’s quality, every comma needs to be observed. If it isn’t, you soon get reminded where it needs to be. It was technically pretty full-on, but wonderful. We built the entirety of the downstairs of Number 10, and it became one of my favourite things I’ve ever done. I’m playing a fictional prime minister. I was lucky enough to meet a real former prime minister to talk about who he could be. In a way, it could be anyone — practically anyone you meet on the street these days. They were very charming and generous. I loved doing it, and I hope people enjoy it. Stephen and Sue — his producing partner and wife — are powerhouses. Sue is one of the best producers the country has ever produced, and Stephen is one of the best writers. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. title: Chris Pratt and Pope Leo Explore St. Peter’s Tomb in Trailer for Vatican Documentary ‘Discovering the Origins’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Oct 16, 2026 6:35am PT Chris Pratt and Pope Leo Explore St. Peter’s Tomb in Trailer for Vatican Documentary ‘Discovering the Origins’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Guillermo del Toro Pays Tribute to Late ‘E.T.’ Designer Carlo Rambaldi Ahead of Hollywood Walk of Fame Honor: ‘A Worldwide Maestro of Magic’ (EXCLUSIVE) 23 hours ago Joanna Hogg to Preside Over El Gouna Film Festival Jury 2 days ago Qatar to Bow Domestic Feature Productions at Upcoming Doha Film Festival in ‘Watershed Moment’ 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source A new documentary pairs Pope Leo and Hollywood star Chris Pratt to delve into the history, religious passion and archaeological discoveries surrounding the tomb of St. Peter at the Vatican. Titled “Pétros Ení — Discovering the Origins,” the doc — which launches from the Rome Film Festival on Friday ahead of its international rollout — marks the 400th anniversary, on Nov. 18, of the consecration of St. Peter’s. Variety can reveal its trailer exclusively above. Related Stories Mark Ruffalo Tells Trump 'Hands Off Our F---ing Vote' or 'I'm Gonna Hulk Out': 'You Won't Like Me When I'm Angry' 'SNL U.K.' Mocks Donald Trump and Andy Burnham's First Meeting, Harvey Weinstein, Sam Altman and More in Wild Weekend Update Featuring footage rarely seen by the general public, it “explores how Peter’s burial place became a center of devotion for early Christians and, eventually, the foundation for the first great basilica built under Emperor Constantine,” as the synopsis puts it. The words “Pétros Ení,” in the title, refer to a Greek inscription than means “Peter is here” found near the apostle’s burial grounds. Pratt, who is best known to audiences for starring in the “Guardians of the Galaxy” and “Jurassic World” franchises, guides viewers on a journey beneath the basilica to discover the history and archaeology of one of Christianity’s most important sites. “The journey culminates with the special participation of Pope Leo XIV, who appears in the film’s final scenes to reflect on Peter and the meaning of his tomb beneath the Basilica,” the synopsis says. “It was an incredible honor to collaborate with Pope Leo and the Vatican on this project,” Pratt said in a statement. “The story of St. Peter is foundational to the Christian faith, and I am deeply grateful for the trust and access I was given to bring his legacy to the screen.” Pope Leo in “Pétros Ení — Discovering the Origins.” Courtesy AF Films, Vatican Media “Pétros Ení — Discovering the Origins” is directed by Spanish filmmaker Paula Ortiz and written by Andrea Tornielli. The doc is produced by AF Films, led by Frank Ariza and Manu Vega, together with Vatican Media and La Fabbrica di San Pietro. The high-profile doc is scheduled to start its international theatrical rollout in February 2027 during the opening weeks of Lent, the Christian season of prayer, reflection and preparation for Easter and the central celebration of the Christian calendar, according to the statement. The rollout will bring together regional distribution partners, with Hallow Studios handling U.S. and Canada distribution; Bosco Films releasing the documentary in Spain; and Cinépolis +Que Cine overseeing its theatrical release in Mexico, Brazil and Colombia. title: El Gouna Artistic Director Andrew Mohsen Puts ‘Discovery’ First: ‘We’re Trying to Draw Attention’ to Overlooked Films
full_text: Oct 16, 2026 6:34am PT El Gouna Artistic Director Andrew Mohsen Puts ‘Discovery’ First: ‘We’re Trying to Draw Attention’ to Overlooked Films By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest 5 Fribourg Film Festival Takeaways, From Audience-Driven Programming to Political Cinema 7 months ago Leon Le on Reframing Vietnam Beyond the Western Gaze: ‘Vietnamese Stories Have Been Told Through a Dated, Disrespectful, Ignorant Lens’ 7 months ago Ukrainian Director Zhanna Ozirna Explores Intimacy Under Siege in ‘Honeymoon’ 7 months ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of El Gouna Film Festival For his first edition at the helm of Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival , artistic director Andrew Mohsen wants to widen the scope of what, and who, audiences discover on the shores of the Red Sea. “Discovery,” Mohsen asserts, sits at the heart of that vision, which builds on the festival’s established place as a showcase for prize winners and standout titles from Cannes, Venice and Berlin, while expanding the emphasis on emerging filmmakers and films that might otherwise escape the spotlight. Related Stories 'SNL' Opens Season With Mamdani Hanging Out With BFF Trump, Natalie Harp Going 'Obsession' Over President Hillary Clinton to Co-Host Podcast on 2026 Midterm Elections With Kara Swisher for Vox Media, Owned by James Murdoch It’s an evolution rather than a break with El Gouna’s past. Succeeding Marianne Khoury, Mohsen, a Cairo International Film Festival vet, who joined the El Gouna programming team in 2023 and later served as head of programming, is looking to deepen the festival’s ties to Arab filmmakers still developing an international profile and to forge stronger connections with filmmakers across Africa, in particular, where the relatively small pool of titles reaching the international festival circuit makes competition for projects particularly intense. Popular on Variety “We are trying to draw attention to the films that didn’t have the same coverage, or the films we feel our audiences need to see,” he tells Variety . Major festivals can screen around a hundred films in a given year, Mohsen notes, yet it is often the prize winners and established directors that remain in the international conversation, while others disappear. A former film critic, Mohsen has attended El Gouna since its 2017 launch. He wants to establish the festival as a go-to meeting point between Arab filmmakers and the international industry and more closely integrate its film selection with CineGouna , its industry and talent-development arm. Internally, that means getting the festival’s various branches working more closely together. Mohsen describes an “open kitchen between us,” with teams exchanging information about filmmakers, projects and guests who could connect with different parts of an increasingly well-established El Gouna network. That effort has become particularly important for Arab cinema . Mohsen says last year El Gouna had just one non-Egyptian Arab film in its narrative competition and one in documentary, its lowest showing for regional cinema since the festival began. Industry-wide competition for films, especially world or regional premieres, is part of the challenge. “We are trying our best to knock on all doors to see how we can expand our connection with the filmmakers,” Mohsen says. Projects backed by other festivals and funds can come with premiere commitments, so El Gouna has responded by investing through its own funding program and approaching filmmakers earlier. Mohsen is also widening the programming scope. Genre cinema has a larger presence this year, a choice he says reflects its growing prominence at major international festivals. Another current emerged across the selection, though not by any explicit design: fear, be it within families, under political regimes, or through anxieties and difficult realities characters themselves struggle to identify. Mohsen points to Miroslav Terzić’s “ Three Weeks After ,” a study of Serbian students confronting the aftermath of a classmate’s death by suicide, as one film in which that unease builds gradually. “You feel you are not really comfortable when you’re watching the film, that there’s something happening, but you cannot put your hand on,” he says. “I find this resonates with what’s happening in the world today.” Another addition is CineGouna Series, led by Egyptian screenwriter Mariam Naoum, an extension of the industry program into an ever more popular medium, both across the region and the wider international entertainment industry. Mohsen sees the move as a natural fit for Egypt, whose television industry has long supplied audiences across the Arab world with on-screen entertainment. “Series, they’re always happening. They’re always selling,” he says. “So we are very strong.” For Mohsen, that strength gives El Gouna an opportunity to invest in a field that remains relatively underrepresented at film festivals in the region. The expansion into series is part of a broader effort to make El Gouna useful to creators beyond simply screening their work. For Mohsen, that means making a case for what the festival can offer filmmakers navigating an increasingly crowded international circuit. “You want exposure, you want connections, you want audiences to react to your film? We can offer all of that.” Asked about the filmmakers he would most like to bring to El Gouna, Mohsen has two names on his wish list: Guillermo del Toro and Park Chan-wook on a festival jury, leading a master class, or simply taking part in the festival. “My two dreams,” he shares. title: How Creators Make Money: Digital-Native Leaders on What Drives Audiences and Brands in the Attention Economy
full_text: Oct 16, 2026 6:15am PT How Creators Make Money: Digital-Native Leaders on What Drives Audiences and Brands in the Attention Economy Variety's 'Strictly Business' podcast features conversations with industry leaders about the business of media and entertainment By Cynthia Littleton Plus Icon Cynthia Littleton Business Editor @Variety_Cynthia Latest FlyDubai Hijacking Incident Set for Development as an Inspirational Movie by Dori Media Group and India’s Sphereorigin 1 day ago YouTube’s Virtues, Industry Consolidation, Christie Brinkley and ‘Baywatch’: Trends and Themes From a Busy Mipcom 1 day ago From Bob Hope to Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to ‘Wicked: One Wonderful Night’: How NBC Became America’s Home for TV Specials 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Variety via Getty Images On the latest episode of Variety ’s “ Strictly Business ” podcast, leaders of top digital-native firms discuss the factors that are funneling viewership, fan engagement and brand deals in the creator economy. Aaron Doades, senior VP of product management for Comscore , Zach Miller, president of JesserCo., Jarret Myer, CEO of Uproxx Studios, and Shaun Newsum, CEO of Culture Genesis, gathered in Los Angeles in September for a session held as part of Variety ‘s annual Entertainment and Technology Summit. This session, and much of the day, was devoted to examining how creators and social video platforms are rewiring our world, especially when it comes to marketing and advertising. Related Stories Trump Taps 'Devoted Fan' Katie Zacharia, a Fox News and CNN Commentator, as White House Press Secretary White House Has Spent More Than $440,000 on Pro-Trump TV Ads Paid for by U.S. Government; Administration Defends 'Unapologetically American' Spots and Denies They're Campaign Ads Myer, a digital media veteran, argues that the rise of superpowers in the creator economy (including sports influencers such as Jesser and IShowSpeed) is a movement back toward a monoculture environment. That’s a counterintuitive take given that the disintermediation of media is driving the upheaval across traditional Hollywood (exhibit A: the newly created Skydance colossus). Popular on Variety Listen to the podcast: “The idea that a creator, an event, a movie, a song can have a moment in culture that everyone’s talking about is happening more and more,” Myer says. “The creator economy is bigger than most people assume it is. They think it’s maybe someone who started a channel in their bedroom, but it’s studios, it’s artists, it’s creators that are all happening outside of the traditional Hollywood formation. More and more, these people are creating the monoculture moments that everyone is talking about. Missing out on that is missing out on the point of entertainment and culture.” Newsum, who leads a creator talent management firm, echoed Myer’s sentiment. “These moments of collective mass consciousness. At Culture Genesis, we call them mini-Super Bowls and they’re happening all the time. And you just don’t know about it,” Newsum says. “The creator economy is always on. There’s content being produced all the time.” Comscore’s Doades pointed to data showing that YouTube is becoming a preferred spot for marketers to find “pockets” of younger viewers who are increasingly hard to find on linear channels, outside of sports. “A lot of folks consume content almost exclusively on creator media. Now, when you’re looking at TV versus creator, the incrementality is massive,” Doades said. “We know that in March of 2026, Jesser had a greater unique reach than 14 live NBA games and the incrementality was 99% — meaning 99% of that audience did not tune in to those NBA games.” Miller in his role helps lead the charge for Jesser, the sports influencer who has enormous cachet with young NBA fans and the league itself. Miller has deep roots in traditional media but he sees no turning back for the content marketplace. “If you’re a marketer and you’re trying to reach a younger audience, you’re going to have a really hard time finding them on television. They’re just not watching TV unless they’re watching live sports,” he says. “But on YouTube, you can find these pockets of audience. The question for advertisers becomes, do you want to spend the money on the traditional media channel that has always been the place to spend it and cross your fingers and hope to find younger audiences there? Or do you need to broaden your strategy, swapping some of that spend on TV for digital channels that will allow you to reach that audience. Or at least expand the spend so that you reach your core audience that you’ve been historically reaching on TV.” (Pictured above, l. to r.: JesserCo.’s Zach Miller, Culture Genius’ Shaun Newsum, Uproxx Studios’ Jarret Myer and Comscore’s Aaron Doades) “Strictly Business” is Variety ’s podcast featuring conversations with industry leaders about the business of media and entertainment. title: Anna Faris Says ‘It Hurts’ After ‘Mom’ Creator Chuck Lorre Admits His ‘Reluctance to Hire’ Her Was Proven ‘Correct’ After She Exited the Show

title: Russell Brand Trial: Second Woman Alleges He Was a ‘Wild-Eyed Maniac’ as He Tried to Pull Her Into Bathroom
full_text: Oct 16, 2026 6:06am PT Russell Brand Trial: Second Woman Alleges He Was a ‘Wild-Eyed Maniac’ as He Tried to Pull Her Into Bathroom By Ellise Shafer Plus Icon Ellise Shafer Latest Russell Brand Trial: Second Woman Alleges He Was a ‘Wild-Eyed Maniac’ as He Tried to Pull Her Into Bathroom 39 minutes ago Jenna Ortega Says She Hopes ‘Klara and the Sun’ Encourages People to ‘Put Down the Computers and Phones’ as Dystopian Film World Premieres in London 15 hours ago Jack O’Connell, Sandra Hüller, Taron Egerton, George MacKay, Rosalind Eleazar, Florian Zeller and More Celebrate London Film Festival at Variety Dinner 21 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source PA Images via Getty Images Russell Brand ‘s criminal trial in London continued on Friday, with his second accuser alleging that Brand was a “wild-eyed maniac” as he tried to pull her into a bathroom. The actor and comedian has been charged with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault relating to incidents with six women spanning from 1999 to 2009. He has pleaded not guilty and denied all allegations against him. Related Stories ‘SNL’ Weekend Update Brutally Mocks Trump for Losing Nobel Peace Prize White House's New AI Website Confirms Trump Lost the 2020 Presidential Election Arriving to Southwark Crown Court, Brand wore a grey suit, white shirt and grey skinny tie. His wife, Laura Gallacher, was by his side again after not attending court on Thursday. He told reporters outside the courthouse that the trial has been an “extraordinary and stressful situation,” according to Sky News . Popular on Variety “But it is also an exploration of truth and justice. As I’ve said before, I pray for everybody involved,” he continued. “It’s in a way very, very sad but hopefully it can bring about some conclusions that are beneficial.” On Friday afternoon, the second alleged victim testified in person from behind a blue screen to protect her identity. In the U.K., all complainants in sexual assault cases are granted automatic lifelong anonymity if they so choose. She said she met Brand while working at MTV in 2001 and complimented his T-shirt, which read “I Am Spartacus,” referencing Stanley Kubrick’s 1960 film. It was “jovial and cheerful banter,” she said, according to Sky News. He then asked her where the bathroom was, and she agreed to show him as she was going that direction anyway. Once they got to the bathroom, “his demeanor changed,” she claimed. He allegedly grabbed her arm “hard” and pleaded with her to “come in, come in, come in,” she added. The woman tried to pull herself away, and said at this point Brand had a “wild look in his eye.” Once she broke free, she called him an “idiot” and then he “gave up” and went into the toilet. After the incident, she questioned how Brand “went from jovial and friendly to this wild-eyed maniac,” according to Sky News. She proceeded to tell two colleagues but not her managers as Brand, who hosted several programs for MTV at the time, was a huge “asset” to MTV and she thought she wouldn’t be believed. Following the Channel 4 documentary that investigated Brand in 2023, she reached out to the police. “I decided I thought it was the right thing to come forward,” she said. The woman was then cross-examined by Brand’s defense lawyer, Ian Winter KC, who claimed that Brand was not pulling her into the bathroom to assault her but rather to have a “consensual” sexual encounter. “Why would you try to drag someone into a toilet unless you wanted to assault them?” she replied. “I was there, I know what happened.” When Winter suggested that her memory of the alleged incident could have been altered by the 2023 media circus surrounding Brand, she said “I knew it was wrong,” adding that the documentary and press coverage “did not change my view of the situation.” On Thursday, the court heard from the first alleged victim via her police video interview. She described in detail an alleged rape by Brand that occurred at the Labour Party conference in 1999 after she met Brand at a cabaret show he was performing in. The woman was then cross-examined in person by Winter, again from behind a screen. The first complainant alleged on Thursday that after talking to Brand at the show, she invited him to come back to her hotel room. She said she thought he was gay at first and felt “sexually safe” with him. However, after she went to the bathroom, the complainant alleges that she emerged to find Brand partially undressed. He demanded that she take photos of him topless — which the court then viewed — and then allegedly raped her. “I was frightened. I remember feeling ‘what on earth have I got myself into’ — and then he did rape me,” she alleged. She claimed that she did say no, but struggled to get him off of her as he was “really heavy.” “I did say no,” she said. “I didn’t want his dirty penis inside me. title: ‘Clayface’ Director James Watkins on Why He “Auditioned the Hell” Out of Star Tom Rhys Harries
full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All October 16, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Tom Rhys Harries attends the world premiere of Warner Bros. 'Clayface' at Hollywood Legion Theater in Los Angeles on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Kevin Winter/Getty Images) Clayface , the new DC Studios film, centers on a Hollywood movie star named Tom Hagen who is left grossly disfigured following a violent attack orchestrated by a Gotham mob boss. Desperate to get that handsome life back, Hagen undergoes an experimental procedure that initially works only to give way to a scary new reality with shape-shifting skin. Enter Clayface. Because it’s a dual role in a body horror thriller, the casting process to find a leading man up to the task was a real beast. “I auditioned the hell out of him,” filmmaker James Watkins told The Hollywood Reporter of finding Mr. Hagen/Clayface in Welsh actor Tom Rhys Harries . “He came in, and I thought he really had something but I wanted to explore it. So we spent time exploring it.” Related Stories Movies DC Studios' 'Clayface': First Reactions Business Barbie's New Boss: Mattel Taps a Warner Bros. Exec to Be Its New Head of Dolls Watkins, speaking at the film’s world premiere on Tuesday night at Hollywood Legion Theater, said he brought in a host of actors but Harries had something special. “I don’t think I’ve ever auditioned anyone that much,” he added. “There was just a sense that Tom had something and [the audition process helped] me explore the character and understand the character.” Harries, who had worked across film and television with credits on such projects as Suspicion, White Lines, The Return, Chewing Gum, Jekyll and Hyde and Unforgotten , had no issues with the lengthy process. “It was spread out over three months and I did two fairly long screen tests with James,” he recalled. “But I’m untested in this space, so I was glad he did it with me really because it meant that we’d had time to workshop the thing before he got onto set.” Harries as Matt Hagen in DC Studios’ Clayface Parisa Taghizadeh/Warner Bros. Pictures Tom Rhys Harries as Matt Hagen and Naomi Ackie as Caitlyn Corr in DC Studios’ Clayface Parisa Taghizadeh/Warner Bros. Pictures Naomi Ackie, who plays the scientist charged with Hagen’s experimental procedure, praised how her co-star shouldered what was a very challenging role. “He’s awesome. He’s hardworking. He comes into the room with so much enthusiasm, but like a lightness. And for this role, it’s actually really hard what he’s doing. I feel like people, when they see it, will understand why,” said Ackie, who also had a front row seat working with another DC star, Robert Pattinson, when they filmed Mickey 17. “He has to go through so many changes, transformations, and he has to track that emotion all the way through and make people kind of love him and want him to win in a way. And he did it with so much grace, so much attention to detail whilst being a really funny, nice guy.” Producer Lynn Harris, who works as Matt Reeves’ producing partner, also touched on the delicate balance Harries had to walk in order to pull off the role. “The idea was to examine a story from Matt Hagen’s perspective with the empathy you might have for this guy who’s just a regular guy that makes a terrible, terrible choice that affects him for the rest of his life. Doing that from a very, very grounded emotional place was an exciting journey to me and to Matt,” she said of the project, which initially came in as a pitch and first draft from horror maestro Mike Flanagan, who eventually had to depart for all of the projects he was juggling from Carrie to the upcoming The Exorcist: Martyrs. Hossein Amini did another draft and Watkins filled in to direct. “Watkins came in and had a great take, and he saw it in the same way that we did in terms of it being super grounded, very emotional, very character driven. It sort of got the core tragedy of the character,” Harries added. Watkins for one can’t wait to see how the film plays when it goes wide because from what he’s seen so far, preview audiences and critics alike are digging it. “It’s a rollercoaster ride. It’s got a lot of horror, a lot of heart, and a lot of humor. It’s a full meal,” he teased. “Look for me, I like horror that gets under people’s skin. I like horror that isn’t just jump scares or mechanical or clockwork. I like horror that’s relatable. And what’s more relatable than our fears for what can happen to our bodies, how they can betray us, all those sorts of things.” So what was the hardest scene for Harries to pull off? “Oh man. The hardest scene was a scene right at the end of the film where I’m lying in a lot of gook and gunk and I was on my last legs,” he said with a smile. “Hopefully it aided the performance.” See for yourself when Clayface opens on Oct. 23. title: Russell Brand Accuser Argues He Wanted To Assault Her When Trying To Drag Her Into A Toilet: “The Intent Was There”
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Russell Brand Accuser Argues He Wanted To Assault Her When Trying To Drag Her Into A Toilet: “The Intent Was There” International Insider: Surfing To MIPCOM Cannes; Russell Brand Trial Begins; Nicole Wallace Interview UK’s Bectu Union Unveils New Chief View All October 16, 2026 5:44am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Russell Brand Getty Russell Brand ‘s second accuser in his trial has argued “intent was there” to assault her when the presenter allegedly tried to drag her into a toilet at the MTV offices in London 25 years ago. The accuser, who we are calling C2, said Brand went from “affable, jovial and friendly” to “suddenly turning into a wild-eyed maniac, trying to pull me into the toilet.” She was working for MTV in London at the time and had been showing Brand where the toilet was, she said. Once she showed him, C2 alleged Brand “was trying to pull me into the bathroom.” Related Stories Legal Russell Brand Trial: Woman Alleges She Was Raped By Star In Hotel Room After He Posed For Semi-Nude Photos News Russell Brand's Accusers: Prosecutors Claim 'Despicable Me' Star Preyed On Women In TV Industry During "Frenzied" & "Wild-Eyed" Incidents “I said, ‘What are you doing? Are you mad? Let me go’, and then he started to plead almost, saying, ‘Go on, go on, come in,'” added C2. “He had hold of my arm hard in a grip and I’m pulling back out towards the corridor.” Watch on Deadline After about 20 seconds, C2, who described herself as “physically stronger than the average woman,” said she was able to “wrench herself away.” She added that she subsequently told two colleagues but didn’t tell her employers as she was “scared” and thought it would be “my word against his.” Brand faces seven charges, encompassing three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault, and one of indecent assault. The charges pertain to allegations made by six women, spanning a decade from 1999 to 2009. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges and has consistently denied wrongdoing. Under cross-examination from Brand’s lawyer, Ian Winter, C2 was questioned over whether at the time she could have actually felt that Brand wanted consensual sex, and it was only after she watched the 2023 documentary Russell Brand: In Plain Sight that she changed her view. C2 denied this. “Why would you drag someone into a toilet if you didn’t want to assault them?,” she added. “You don’t drag someone by the arm. You don’t grip someone and try and pull them. That’s not consensual. The intent was there. It could have been very different.” As they were walking towards the toilet before the incident, C2 said “nothing was suggested about romance, not a word.” She added that even though he was one of the flagship MTV presenters at the time, she did not see Brand again while working at the network. She did not come forward before seeing the documentary because “in 2001, it would have been my word against his,” C2 said, adding: “I had a job to consider, [and] came away relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me, and I managed to get myself out the situation. I just wanted a quiet life. I didn’t need this.” “Sex was a huge preoccupation for him” Yesterday, a police interview was played to the court from complainant C1, who alleged Brand raped her in his hotel room during the 1999 Labour Party conference in Bournemouth after he posed for semi-nude photos from her. He was appearing in a play at the time on the fringes of the conference. Today, a number of witnesses gave evidence supporting C1. John Rogers, who wrote a play Brand appeared in at the Labour conference, said the presenter had told him he had had an “encounter” with a woman that week. Brand’s “reaction was a bit odd” and “he was a bit flustered” when telling the story, according to Rogers. A flatmate of Brand’s during the Bournemouth conference, Andrew Dobson, alleged Brand wanted to leave hurriedly the morning after the alleged assault took place. “He came in and there was suddenly an urgency,” added Dobson. “It felt tense and confusing. I didn’t understand why.” Dobson said “sex was a huge preoccupation” for the Forgetting Sarah Marshall star. Before finding fame, he described Brand as “vibrant, egotistical, lively, demanding, persuasive and erratic.” Two acquaintances of C1’s also told the court via witness statement that she had told them about her alleged rape after watching the Brand documentary in 2023. One said C1 had told her she had been raped previously by her husband “and felt as if she were reliving this and completely froze” during the alleged assault. C1 told her she was worried about backlash from her community if she reported Brand at the time, this acquaintance said. The other said she was told by C1 over WhatsApp after C1 had reported Brand to the police. The police had told her she should only share the information with “trusted persons,” this witness said, via a pre-written statement. The trial continues. title: From ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ To Scottish Indie Boss: Kevin McKidd On Ferryman Films & His New Show ‘The Only Suspect’
full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart BBC Studios’ Boss Says Streaming Is The Future But Linear Still Pays The Bills MIPCOM 2026 Takeaways: Surfing The New Wave Of TV With YouTube, ‘Baywatch’, Skydance, Banijay & More How Matthew Gray Gubler Went Back To The Drawing Board For ‘Einstein’ View All October 16, 2026 5:33am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kevin McKidd in 'The Only Suspect' Red Planet Pictures, David Hindley Scottish multi-hyphenate Kevin McKidd has launched an indie on home turf, and says he’s using his Hollywood experience to make it work. When Deadline speaks with him in his New York hotel, McKidd is in the throes of filming Conviction , the Elisabeth Moss-starring Hulu legal drama from House creator David Shore. After that, he’s headed to L.A. to direct some episodes of ABC’s Grey’s Anatomy , the show in which he starred as Dr. Owen Hunt before he said goodbye to the role in 2026 after almost two decades. Meanwhile, he’s recently wrapped on UK drama The Only Suspect . Related Stories News Sky-ITV: UK Culture Secretary "Minded To Intervene" Over $2.1B Merger News ITV Buys 'The Galway Bay Murders' Thriller Starring Kate Mulgrew & Colm Meaney In Conviction McKidd plays the husband of Moss’ Neve Harper, a confident lawyer who finally has her shot at a career-making case: a high-profile murder where the husband is accused of killing his wife by setting their home on fire. Watch on Deadline The conversation, however, quickly turns to his native Scotland. McKidd is using the smarts he learned in the U.S. business to power up Ferryman Films , his indie label out of Edinburgh. “I’ve got access to this American skillset and these people who’ve been showrunners on big shows,” he says, “and then there are these Scottish writers with all this potential. It’s really been fun to see that cross-pollination.” One project he’s working on but keeping mum about is Troubadour. “We’re developing that with Bruno Heller ( Rome ) who is the chieftain of it, but Kieran Hurley, who’s quite an accomplished Scottish playwright, is co-writing with him,” McKidd says. His new indie banner has partnered with STV Studios, the production and distribution arm of Scottish broadcaster STV run by former NBCUniversal exec David Mortimer. An adaptation of William Shaw detective novel The Red Shore is the first collaboration resulting from the deal. There’s also Friends Like These for the BBC in the works, a female-led show about a group of 30-something friends. Gillian McCormack ( Counsels ) is writing. A Guilty Secret One thing that has wrapped is psychological drama The Only Suspect , adapted by Simon Ashdown ( Trigger Point ) from the novel by Louise Candlish . It is for ITV in the U.K., with Farren Blackburn directing. Moving between the present day and mid-1990s London, it follows Alex (McKidd) and his wife, Beth, played by Amaka Okafor ( Black Rabbit ). The devoted couple’s seemingly picture-perfect suburban life hides a devastating truth linked to a dead body—Alex, it transpires, is the man who buried that body, and has been harboring the dark secret ever since. The Only Suspect Red Planet Pictures, David Hindley “He’s very much a kind of antihero,” McKidd says of his character. “That’s a really delicious challenge—to have an audience root for a character while also having major mixed feelings about them. I find those characters a fantastic knot to untie.” The setting for the 1990s part of the series is Camden, London, which was very much the epicenter of the U.K.’s Cool Britannia movement. It struck a chord with McKidd, given he was one of the stars of Trainspotting , a defining movie of that era. He played the memorable and tragic character of Tommy in the Danny Boyle film and recently attended a 30 th anniversary screening of the film in Edinburgh. “I spent my formative years exactly in the period of time in which we see the younger versions of these characters,” McKidd says. “I didn’t kill anyone, thankfully,” he quips. “But there are those mistakes that you make in your twenties as you’re figuring out life, which is what this show is all about. I was able to get into that character because it weirdly reflected my own life, going back to this place in the same way as Alex as he has to go back and face what happened in the 90s.” McKidd says viewers should buckle up for twists and turns. “Every episode keeps you guessing. Just when you think you know what’s happening, they pull the rug from under you. It has quite a dark psychology, but there’s a lot of humor in it too.” Red Planet Pictures is producing. The venerable U.K. label is majority-owned by Fremantle, which is handling international sales and will be pushing at MIPCOM. It is Red Planet’s second Candlish adaptation after Our House, one of ITV’s biggest new drama launches back in 2022. Explaining why McKidd was such a good fit for The Only Suspect , Red Planet’s Tom Mullens, who is an exec producer on the show, says: “He’s such a clever actor with great dramatic range and a chameleon-like versatility, which was essential for the part of Alex, a deeply complex character who goes on a cathartic journey across the four episodes. “Not only do we see a charming and manipulative Alex as he protects his secret, but we also see a man who loves his wife and is faced with an impossible choice, knowing that by confronting his guilt and telling the truth, he might also destroy his life and marriage.” Heading Home McKidd starred in several U.K.-produced shows during his time on Grey’ s Anatomy but still noticed a change when it came to filming The Only Suspect . Grey’s Anatomy ABC, Scott Everett White “On [ Grey’s Anatomy ] we have three cameras rolling all the time, every take. But with The Only Suspect it was a single camera, which is pretty much where I started, in indie films in the ’90s and the early 2000s. “With three cameras, it can dilute what you’re doing. [Director] Farren Blackburn and the DP did such a good job at using that one camera and always placing it in the optimal position to get the most intense version of that setup.” McKidd’s own directing work has made him more of a team player. “Before, I was probably a bit of a pain in the arse. I was like ‘You know, my character wouldn’t do that.’ Now I’m much more accommodating. I know what it is like to sit in that director’s chair.” With experience in front of and behind the camera, he says he’s also happy to relinquish control when an acting gig comes up. “When I worked with Ben Williams, who was brilliant [as the director of Hideo Yokoyama adaptation Six Four ], and Farren, the first thing I said to them was, ‘I’m not going to come in as this actor-director who’s going to be rolling his eyes at your choices. I can take that chip in my brain out and just focus on being an actor. I’m just going to put my complete trust in you.’” Being an indie boss, meanwhile, is another skillset. It requires patience as the options are picked up, writers are attached and pitches made to buyers. “I’ve got this underpinning of being a theater actor, really, who fell into all this TV and film,” McKidd says. “Then I was plugged into the Hollywood system, having come from very independent grassroots. I’ve got one foot in both camps, and that can benefit my acting, but also the company.” With Conviction calling, McKidd signs off: “I’m always trying to be a moving target. That’s what I want for the company. I want to keep people guessing.” Netflix Shakeup: Bajaria’s Exit Signals Changes To Come As Rice Hire Elicits Praise Steven Soderbergh To Work With Matt Reeves On Final Weeks Of ‘The Batman II’ Shoot Tim Burton And ‘Klara And The Sun’ Author Kazuo Ishiguro’s Secret Project ‘Street Fighter’ $4M Previews, A24 Holmes Doc Draws $2M Read More About: Comments

title: Comics Accuse Hot AI Fakes of Stealing Their Jokes Word for Word to Push OnlyFans Pages
full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All October 16, 2026 5:32am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The real George Brett Olson is at left. AI is coming for your jokes — and its armed with double Ds. Two comics have posted videos within the past couple of weeks showing sexy AI “comedians” on social media racking up views by performing their exact routines. First was comic and content creator, George Brett Olson, who did a breakdown (watch it below) accusing an AI Instagram account with 300,000 followers of seemingly ripped off his joke word for word. The fake comic was a highly realistic-looking female character that even had the same venue background and wore clothing similar to his own. The avatar also, he noted, has an OnlyFans page. Related Stories Business Disney Circles Character.ai as Chatbot Company Files For Chapter 11 Bankruptcy Business Netflix Has Used AI on About 300 Titles, but "Human Touch Is Critical," Exec Says in Busan “AI stole my joke and my outfit,” Olson said. “You might be saying, ‘I’ve heard comedians talk about this already,’ but this is new — very new.” Adding to the surreal nature of the incident, Olson’s joke was about AI’s threat to jobs and how billionaires like Instagram’s parent company co-founder Mark Zuckerberg are complicit. “This is the most ironic thing that’s ever happened to me,” Olson said. A few days ago, stand-up comic Julia Jasunas ( Comics Unleashed ) took to Instagram to show a similar side-by-side example of an AI account with 250,000 followers ripping off one of her jokes verbatim (below). The fake comic even made the same random aside that Jasunas said to a member of her audience. “So another AI bot just stole my joke,” Jasunas said. “I’ve seen a couple other videos of other comedians posting about the exact same problem, and the thing that’s the most concerning is these AI bots are going viral, and people think that they’re real people.” The AI version was seemingly crafted to look like a stand-up comic version of Lara Croft. “Who does comedy in Daisy Duke shorts?” Jasunas quipped. UK comedy news site Chortle found several other examples of stolen jokes on the same account that knocked off Jasunas — including content by Char Ramtin, Olivia Carter and Hannah Berner. “It’s incredibly unsettling that someone is using scantily clad AI-generated women to perform stolen jokes and generate profit from views and engagement, then funnel people toward an OnlyFans account for additional profit, all for a woman who doesn’t even exist!” Jasunas told the site. “No wonder there’s a male loneliness epidemic.” (Neither AI Instagram account cited by the comics replied to a request for comment). Two of the AI-generated comedians Olson and Jasunas said they have received no support from Meta regarding the issue and Olson blasted the platform for not doing more to protect original content. “The craziest thing is that there’s no terms of service violation here,” he said. “We’re watching [social media leaders] in real time say, ‘Hey, we’re building something that’s going to destroy everything,’ and then watching them protect no one [and] not anything that makes us human — songs, laughter … Maybe [Meta] should realize the reason we like the internet is that low key we like each other … and now you’re going to exponentially flood the internet with things that are not us.” In response to an inquiry by The Hollywood Reporter , Instagram chief Adam Mosseri said in a statement, “I don’t think it’s practical for us to try and ban AI content from the platform. It’s gonna be harder and harder to identify, and it’s not all bad content (though yes, there is plenty of slop). But we are very invested in trying to drive more traffic to original content creators, and if an AI creator is ripping off content wholesale, it would be good for us to work out what we can do about that. I’m not sure what it would be, but I’ll make sure to talk to the team and look into it.” A Meta spokesperson added the problem has cropped up on other platforms (such as YouTube and Tiktok) as well. Jasunas, meanwhile, urged those watching her video to support comics by going to see live shows instead of scrolling for clips “Comedians post their stand-up clips online to get you to come out and see live comedy,” Jasunas added. “Live comedy is meant to be experienced in the flesh, and if you’re watching these videos and you’re not realizing that these are computers regurgitating our jokes that we’ve crafted over time on stage and honed and whittled down into a punchy bit. Then you need to get out and take a walk and go see a live show.” View this post on Instagram View this post on Instagram THR

title: Omar Sy on Taking Creative Control of Netflix’s ‘Lupin’ and Why ‘Black Dumas’ Will Spark Political Debate in France
full_text: Oct 16, 2026 5:22am PT Omar Sy on Taking Creative Control of Netflix’s ‘Lupin’ and Why ‘Black Dumas’ Will Spark Political Debate in France By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest Omar Sy on Taking Creative Control of Netflix’s ‘Lupin’ and Why ‘Black Dumas’ Will Spark Political Debate in France 1 hour ago YouTube’s Virtues, Industry Consolidation, Christie Brinkley and ‘Baywatch’: Trends and Themes From a Busy Mipcom 1 day ago Mediawan’s Pierre-Antoine Capton on Buying Reese Witherspoon’s Hello Sunshine and Doubling Down on Hollywood Amid Consolidation (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Selly Sy/Netflix Netflix ‘s smash hit heist series “ Lupin ” is back bigger and bolder after three years, and its French star Omar Sy , who plays French gentleman thief Assane Diop, has something to do with it. Sy, who served as artistic producer on previous installments, makes his debut as co-showrunner alongside Louis Leterrier for the show’s fourth part, on top of co-producing it through their joint banner Carrousel Studios. Related Stories Trump Says Execution of Fort Hood Shooter by Firing Squad Will Not Be Livestreamed Judge Extends Block on Trump's White House Ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico Speaking in an interview with Variety ahead of the Oct. 23 launch, Sy revealed he made greater creative control a condition of his return on the show. Popular on Variety “There were quite a few moments in previous seasons when I felt frustrated because things I wanted didn’t necessarily end up on screen. So my condition for continuing was that I would have a little more say in the decisions. They gave me that role, and it allowed me to change things,” Sy said during the zoom interview, sitting against a red backdrop of “Lupin” featuring an animated silhouette of Diop and the Eiffel Tower. The new season picks up four years after the events of Part 3, with Assane behind bars before finding himself targeted by a mysterious copycat who pulls off a string of elaborate heists in his name. With a bigger budget from Netflix, Sy and Leterrier leaned further into the show’s superhero-like qualities, expanding its universe beyond the novels of Maurice Leblanc and weaving some futuristic elements. “We’re moving a little further away from Maurice Leblanc…. We brought it more into our own universe,” said Sy. “That’s why we’re going further into the prison setting, introducing new technologies and all these different elements. We’re embracing modernity, whether it’s through the prison itself or all the technology that the copycat uses to trap Assane.” Emmanuel Guimier/Netflix The challenge, Sy says, was to preserve what made “Lupin” a global hit while making the new season feel fresh enough to draw in viewers who have never watched the series. The new role also allowed Sy to bring in rising French actor Théo Christine and explore more emotional side of Assane’s story, Sy, who’s currently shooting Bradley Cooper’s Ocean prequel alongside Margot Robbie, has carved out a career in Hollywood and in European cinema, often serving as a producer on projects exploring social and political issues. He starred in and produced Mathieu Vadepied’s “Father & Soldier,” which shed light on the largely overlooked history of Senegalese soldiers who fought for France during WWI. His upcoming French projects include Ladj Ly’s “Dumas: Diable Noir” (“Black Dumas”), which reunites him with Christine and tells the story of Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, the formerly enslaved man who became France’s first Black general and whose son would go on to become one of the country’s most celebrated writers. Slated for release in October 2027, “Black Dumas” will arrive just months after France’s presidential election, which is shaping up to be one of the country’s most divisive in decades, with the far right leading polls and political tensions running high. “One thing I’m sure of is that ‘Dumas’ is going to generate a lot of debate and discussion,” said Sy, who’s lived in Los Angeles for years but still votes in France. “We need conversations right now. I just hope they can be calm, thoughtful conversations rather than heated ones.” While he had broken through with his first leading role in the French comedy “Intouchables,” it’s his part as Assane Diop in “Lupin” which turned Sy into an international star in 2021. Like “Emily in Paris,” “Lupin” has contributed to boosting tourism in the French capital, and has been hugely successful internationally on Netflix, although the latter has even more merit, being in French. You’re co-showrunner on this season. What made you want to get more involved creatively, and how did that change the way you worked on the series? The truth is, I’ve been involved in the same way from the very beginning. My involvement hasn’t changed. I’ve always been part of all the conversations, from the first to the last. The difference is that before, I was allowed to participate and make suggestions, but I couldn’t make the decisions or necessarily see those ideas through. There were quite a few moments in previous seasons when I felt frustrated because things I wanted didn’t necessarily end up on screen. So my condition for continuing was that I would have a little more say in the decisions. They gave me that role, and it allowed me to change things. For example, bringing in Théo Christine was something we wanted to do, and we went after him. There are decisions like that which might seem quite radical but can take the show somewhere different. That’s what this new role has allowed me to do. But in terms of my involvement, it’s been the same from the start. I just have a little more decision-making power now. Emmanuel Guimier/Netflix I found the father-son relationship with Théo Christine in the first episode incredibly moving. You also worked together with this young actor on Ladj Ly’s “Dumas: Diable Noir,” didn’t you? What’s funny is that actually happened afterward. We approached Théo for “Lupin,” and he said yes. Then, while we were working on the series, he got the role in “Dumas.” The first episode feels more dramatic than previous seasons, especially with the father-son relationship. Was that something you particularly wanted to explore? What’s great about this series is that you have a bit of everything. There’s drama, but there’s also comedy, lighter moments, flamboyant characters and all the action that comes with it. It’s really a place where you can put so many different things. That’s why I always say that “Lupin” is my favorite toy. You can turn it in every direction, you can do all sorts of things in the same universe and with the same character. Were you also interested in exploring the prison setting more extensively this season? Yes, because ultimately we’re dealing with a thief, and prison is part of that world. It’s something we hadn’t really explored before. In the first season, there’s a short sequence where he’s in prison, and we also touch on that world through his father, but we’d never really gone into it in depth. This time, we wanted to explore it further, and we also filmed it a little differently. The prison almost has a futuristic, science-fiction quality. It feels quite stylized. We brought it more into our own universe. That’s really what this season does. We’re fully embracing the world we’ve created. That’s why we’re going further into the prison setting, introducing new technologies and all these different elements. We’re moving a little further away from Maurice Leblanc and bringing more of our own ideas into it. We’re embracing modernity, whether it’s through the prison itself or all the technology that the copycat uses to trap Assane. The production looks bigger and more ambitious. Did you have a significantly larger budget this time? We definitely had more resources. And we have to acknowledge that, because Netflix would be very upset if we said otherwise! They gave us the means to make this season, and it was important to us that you could see and feel that on screen. There’s almost a superhero quality to this season, particularly with the idea of Lupin versus Lupin. It feels a little like a Marvel movie. Yes, but actually, when I say we’re moving away from Maurice Leblanc, that’s one area where we’re not. He did that several times himself. He brought in Sherlock Holmes, and at one point Lupin even faces another Lupin. Maurice Leblanc had already done that. I think it’s Marvel that copied Maurice Leblanc! But seriously, from the very beginning, when we decided to bring Lupin back and make this series, that’s how we imagined the character. Louis [Leterrier] decided to film him using those codes. That’s why his coat is like a cape. We really conceived this character as a superhero. It’s also why you have those shots of him on the rooftops of Paris, with his silhouette against the skyline, almost like a shadow. That superhero dimension has always been part of our vision of the character, and we fully embrace it. I’ve only seen the first episode, but I already suspect that Assane’s best friend might have something to do with what’s going on. Is betrayal one of the central themes of this season? With “Lupin,” there’s always betrayal somewhere. It’s a battle of wits, a game of intelligence, and we need those twists. Very often, betrayal is part of that. One of the things I love about this series is that we established something in the first season that continues to work today: speculation. Everyone is trying to figure out who’s behind everything. It’s like a game of Cluedo, trying to guess who the killer is. I love that. It’s one of my favorite aspects of the series. That whole whodunit element is something we deliberately work on. It’s part of the pleasure of “Lupin,” both for us and for the audience. I feel that quite a few films and series have tried to copy “Lupin” in recent years. I’m not the one saying it! You said it, not me! Has the success of “Lupin” made you want to become more involved in creating other films and series, beyond acting and producing? Yes, absolutely. That’s exactly what we’re working on with Thomas [Benski], Louis [Leterrier] and Carrousel Studios. We’re developing projects that I hope we’ll be able to announce soon. Carrousel really came out of everything we experienced together on “Lupin.” Louis and I discovered each other artistically through this series. At a certain point, we reached another level in our collaboration, and we realized that together we were capable of creating these kinds of projects. Carrousel is really about taking that collaboration further and doing it on a much bigger scale. We’re working on things, and I hope we’ll soon be able to come out with an idea that is still cooking at the moment. What’s also remarkable about this new season of “Lupin” is that someone who has never seen the series could start watching with Part 4 and still get into it. Was making it accessible to new audiences important to you? Thank you, because that’s exactly what we wanted to achieve. That’s also why we took our time. Obviously, we’re continuing a series that has been watched by a lot of people, so there are things we had to preserve. But at the same time, we had to bring something new. Finding that balance was really the challenge, and it’s something we worked on enormously. So hearing you say that is very satisfying, because it’s exactly what we were trying to do. You’ve had a busy year. You starred in “Dumas: Diable Noir,” and you’re also shooting the new “Ocean’s” movie. Have you finished filming that? No, we’re still filming. Can you tell me anything about your character? I can’t! You know how these things work. You can’t really talk about anything until someone tells you exactly what you can say. And since we’re still shooting, I’m keeping quiet. You know what you know, and I can’t tell you anything more. But I can tell you we’re still working on it. We shot over the summer, and we’re now finishing it. It’s great. What’s Bradley Cooper like as a director? Bradley is someone who’s incredibly inspired. He’s very involved, very passionate. He’s completely immersed in what he’s doing. He really enjoys his work and throws himself into it. And because he’s also an actor, he has a way of communicating what he wants that makes it very easy for another actor to understand and deliver. I’d already worked with him as an actor on “Burnt.” Even back then, he was someone who shared a lot with the people around him. Now that he’s also behind the camera, it’s a real pleasure. It’s incredibly inspiring to watch him work. And because I’m also interested in exploring what’s happening behind the camera, particularly as a producer, seeing the way he approaches and invests himself in every aspect of a project is very inspiring for me. You’ve been working in Hollywood for several years now. Are there still things you’re particularly eager to do in the U.S. that you haven’t had the chance to do yet? I don’t really think that way. I don’t approach my career by telling myself that there’s a particular box I still need to tick. That’s not how I function at all. I started in this business with a certain momentum, and I’ve tried to keep moving without making too many plans or calculations. There are encounters, opportunities, things that inspire you. I see it as a movement that continues rather than something that needs to be planned out. Take Carrousel, for example. It started with my meeting Louis, then Thomas, and that led to Carrousel. It’s the same with Bradley. We met on “Burnt,” we got along really well, and today he’s calling me to work with him on this new project. That’s how things happen for me. I don’t sit down and think that I need to do this or that next. It’s not my way of working. The things I do come more from my gut than from my head. What’s interesting about the U.S. industry right now is that alongside all the consolidation, with Paramount and Warner Bros., there are also a lot of independent companies and extraordinary creative talent. That’s what I believe in more. I believe in what’s being created a little on the margins, with lighter, more flexible structures that are more focused on creativity and on bringing something new. Because on the other side, the studios are becoming bigger and bigger. But the more they merge, the more they become fixed and rigid. What’s exciting about creating things is that sense of freedom, that lightness and the ability to adapt. And coming back to Carrousel, that’s exactly what we want to preserve: the ability to move quickly and adapt quickly. You also have Ladj Ly’s “Dumas: Diable Noir” coming out next year, possibly around the time of the French elections. Given the political climate, do you think a film like that could have a particular resonance? What role can cinema play in these debates? One thing I’m sure of is that “Dumas” is going to generate a lot of debate and discussion. For me, that’s also one of the things cinema can do. It’s not its only purpose, obviously, but it can create conversations. When you make a film like “Dumas,” that’s also something you hope to provoke. And given the current political context, I do think a film like this will generate discussion. We need conversations right now. I just hope they can be calm, thoughtful conversations rather than heated ones. You’re still based in Los Angeles, right? Yes, I’m still in the United States. So you’re watching what’s happening in France from a distance? No, I’m not watching from a distance. I’m here, I’m right in the middle of it, and I feel what’s happening. Although you have plenty of problems in the U.S. as well. The thing is, the problems in the United States aren’t my problems. My problems are here. So your heart is still in Paris? Obviously.
