title: ‘Toy Story 5’ Co-Director Kenna Harris on Going From Jessie Superfan to Pixar Filmmaker — and the Two-Week Rewrite That Reshaped the Sequel
full_text: Oct 16, 2026 5:17am PT ‘Toy Story 5’ Co-Director Kenna Harris on Going From Jessie Superfan to Pixar Filmmaker — and the Two-Week Rewrite That Reshaped the Sequel By Davide Abbatescianni Plus Icon Davide Abbatescianni Latest ‘Toy Story 5’ Co-Director Kenna Harris on Going From Jessie Superfan to Pixar Filmmaker — and the Two-Week Rewrite That Reshaped the Sequel 1 hour ago ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ VFX Boss Jerome Chen on Hulk’s Redesign, Finishing 445 Shots in a Week 1 day ago Laika’s ‘Wildwood’ VFX Supervisor Steve Emerson Details the Making of Travis Knight’s Stop-Motion Epic 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kenna Harris walking an audience through 'Toy Story 5' at View Conference, Oct. 16, 2026 Long before co-directing Pixar’s “ Toy Story 5 ,” Kenna Harris spent childhood afternoons drawing Jessie, painstakingly reproducing details from “Toy Story 2” and even imagining Woody offering the cowgirl a flower. Decades later, the character helped Harris navigate a daunting first feature — including a two-week production pause to overhaul a story that was not yet working. “She was my cowgirl through and through,” Harris said at View Conference in Turin on Friday, displaying childhood fan art and explaining how Jessie’s boldness became a guiding principle while making the film with director Andrew Stanton . Related Stories 'SNL U.K.' Mocks Donald Trump and Andy Burnham's First Meeting, Harvey Weinstein, Sam Altman and More in Wild Weekend Update Mayor Zohran Mamdani Refuses Jimmy Kimmel’s Request to Text Trump a Selfie of Them Stanton invited Harris to co-direct in late 2022, after work on “Luca,” “Ciao Alberto” and “Inside Out 2.” Harris accepted, then asked to co-write the screenplay despite never having tackled a feature script. “Who was I to put myself in a position this precarious, where I could very well fail in front of the man who wrote my entire childhood?” Harris recalled. The collaboration ultimately earned Harris a screenwriting credit alongside Stanton. Popular on Variety That willingness to take risks extended to campaigning for Jessie and Buzz to kiss amid a perilous action sequence. “I just think there should be a ton of action, and it should be perilous, and then they should kiss super duper hard,” Harris remembered telling Stanton, who agreed. Another image — Jessie riding a real horse — helped inspire the ranch setting and a new character, Blaze. Harris, production designer Bob Pauley and the story team visited BreyerFest, a Kentucky convention devoted to model horses, for research. The filmmakers also had to find the right approach to Lilypad, the tablet threatening Bonnie’s attachment to traditional toys. Harris rejected the notion of an irredeemably evil device: the story needed to acknowledge how difficult it is for children and adults alike to escape technology’s grip. But the early versions still failed to deliver an emotionally compelling journey. “We stopped production for two weeks, and focused on the film’s core issue at the time,” Harris said. “Our act one was not working.” The first week was devoted to diagnosing the problem; during the second, Harris and Stanton raced to rewrite. Initially, Jessie’s overriding goal was simply to win back playtime with Bonnie, especially after becoming separated from her during a dance class. But early screenings showed that audiences were unmoved by a conflict that echoed the first film’s competition for a child’s attention. “The stakes of losing playtime felt too soft,” Harris explained. The breakthrough was to make Bonnie’s loneliness the emotional engine. Jessie, whose painful history with her former owner Emily was already established, would instead strive to help the shy girl make a real friend. Blaze, previously more peripheral to the adventure, became essential. “This was the moment that turned an okay movie into a good one,” Harris said, recalling a noticeable improvement in reactions at internal screenings. Another discarded approach had Jessie meet an elderly Emily at her former home. Harris felt it resolved the character’s pain too neatly. The filmmakers instead returned to the tire-swing tree from “Toy Story 2,” building a more understated climax around a time capsule. Harris recalled seeing the revised ending at a screening and realizing, “There’s no way we’re changing it.” The decision to put Jessie front and center was itself contested. “Part of the risk of this film was having Jessie as the protagonist,” Harris revealed, recalling questions about whether audiences would rather watch Woody and Buzz. The filmmakers held firm: those characters would remain important, but Jessie’s emotional history gave the sequel its purpose. Harris also helped shape the movie’s imagination sequences, pushing Pixar’s artists toward more spontaneous, painterly images rather than the studio’s usual meticulous realism. “We wanted to lean into something that felt more ephemeral and fleeting,” Harris said. Rapid experiments in lighting, movement and effects became part of a process the crew called “playtime weeklies.” The approach reflected a larger lesson in directing: learning to delegate, invite others into difficult decisions and leave space for play. Stanton’s guiding idea for the film was that “our limited time with others can impact a lifetime,” a theme that spoke both to Jessie’s journey and to Harris’ own time at Pixar. “I wanted people to know that I was here,” Harris said of the desire to leave a personal imprint on a beloved franchise. By the end of production, that fear had given way to confidence. “I look back now, and I can see that I was here.” Why Netflix, Amazon and Other Streamers Have Not Proved Saviors for the Kids Content Industry ‘The Monster of Florence’ Director Stefano Sollima on ‘Completely Different’ Second Chapter of Netflix’s Hit Serial Killer Series: ‘A Very Complex Story to Tell’ (EXCLUSIVE) Netflix Film VP Doug Belgrad Is Out Amid Layoffs ‘Bridgerton’ Spinoff, Centered on Lady Violet, Ordered by Netflix ‘East of Eden’ Hits 6.5 Million Views in Four Days on Netflix ‘A Different World’ Renewed for Season 2 at Netflix Loading comments...

title: Netflix Is Profitable and Still Growing. Why Did It Just Make a Huge Round of Layoffs and Oust Its Top Content Exec?
full_text: Oct 16, 2026 5:15am PT Netflix Is Profitable and Still Growing. Why Did It Just Make a Huge Round of Layoffs and Oust Its Top Content Exec? By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Netflix Is Profitable and Still Growing. Why Did It Just Make a Huge Round of Layoffs and Oust Its Top Content Exec? 2 hours ago Skydance’s Market Value Is Currently Less Than Half What Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount Combined Were Worth 18 hours ago Comcast Donated $7.5 Million for Donald Trump’s Lavish New White House Ballroom 20 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michael Haddad for Variety In 2025, Netflix notched a net profit of $11 billion on a 16% increase in revenue, to $46.6 billion. It expects revenue growth to cool off this year, projecting an increase of 13%-14%, while the streamer is aiming to boost operating margin by 200 basis points, to 31.5%. It has a healthy balance sheet, with $9.1 billion in cash and equivalents and very manageable total debt of $14.4 billion as of June 30. So why did Netflix, which is still throwing off a good chunk of change, this week lay off around 1,000 employees — its biggest cutback to date? Related Stories Pro-Trump Ads Funded With Taxpayer Dollars Air on CNN and MS NOW; White House Has Spent $2.9 Million on the TV Spots to Date 'SNL' Opens Season With Mamdani Hanging Out With BFF Trump, Natalie Harp Going 'Obsession' Over President Companies often make layoffs in crisis mode, such as when they’re facing near-term revenue shortfalls and they simply can’t make payroll. That’s not the case here. But Netflix faces a festering pain point. Popular on Variety Specifically, investors are worried about the slowdown in its U.S./Canada region — which has raised questions about its long-term growth trajectory. For the second quarter of 2026, Netflix’s UCAN revenue decelerated from 14% the prior quarter to 10% (partially due to its recent price hikes ). The company also issued Q3 revenue guidance below analyst expectations. Shares of Netflix are down 20% year-to-date on fears the streamer’s days of double-digit gains are coming to an end. Netflix’s 6% reduction in force and the move to boot chief content officer Bela Bajaria — replacing her with well-regarded industry veteran Peter Rice, who hails from Disney and 21st Century Fox — signal its attempts to get in front of the issue. Multiple industry sources told Variety they think Bajaria is being made the scapegoat for Netflix’s larger problems. But content is the main engine that powers Netflix’s financials. As Variety ’s analysis of Bajaria’s exit noted, Netflix hasn’t produced a “culture-defining hit in the vein of ‘Stranger Things’ in quite some time.” Back to the all-important UCAN region: Total viewing hours in the U.S. and Canada declined in Q2, according to BMO Capital Markets analyst Brian Pitz. Netflix’s parting ways with Bajaria and hiring Rice “suggest[s] to us that engagement trends may have softened further in 3Q26E,” Pitz said in a research note Friday. The change in content leadership prompted the Wall Street firm to lower revenue estimates for Netflix’s Q3 and Q4 by around 1% each and to also reduce its 2027 revenue forecast by 1.5%. BMO’s model, Pitz added, “conservatively does not assume a UCAN revenue acceleration” until 2029. Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos, in a memo to staff Thursday about the executive shake-up, seemed to acknowledge that the company needs a more robust content lineup in the U.S./Canada region. Sarandos wrote that he sees “an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in UCAN where we have an outsize impact in creating big, buzzy hits that our members love and drive conversation around the world.” And what about the tranche of 1,000 employees being laid off? Sarandos and co-chief Greg Peters told staffers in a companywide memo the job cuts are part of giving it the means to “invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation.” Note that Netflix isn’t alone in handing out pink slips. Disney — also profitable — has made three rounds of layoffs in 2026 across different parts of the business. Unlike Netflix, Disney is wrestling with the ongoing deterioration of linear TV. But echoing Netflix’s explanation for its RIF, CEO Josh D’Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston have told the Street they’re looking to cut costs, including through layoffs, to “create incremental capacity to invest for growth.” Netflix’s top brass will surely be asked for more detail on the restructuring (and their decision to swap out Bajaria for Rice) when it reports Q3 earnings next Tuesday, Oct. 20. That will be the kickoff to an intriguing quarterly earnings season for the entertainment sector, which will include the first print from David Ellison’s freshly minted Skydance — poised to ax thousands of staffers after the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. title: International Insider: Surfing To MIPCOM Cannes; Russell Brand Trial Begins; Nicole Wallace Interview
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max International Insider: Surfing To MIPCOM Cannes; Russell Brand Trial Begins; Nicole Wallace Interview Layoffs Take Place At ‘The Repair Shop’ Producer Ricochet UK’s Bectu Union Unveils New Chief View All October 16, 2026 5:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Baywatch' Michael Decker Welcome back Insiders, glad to have you here after a busy week in Cannes and plenty else going on. Sign up here and whatever you do, read on. Surfing To MIPCOM Cannes Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images Newly minteds: At this year’s MIPCOM there was a little bit of surf and a whole lot of shine as the edition was dominated by Fox and Fremantle’s Baywatch reboot, along with two newly-minted players emerging at their first big international market. While Baywatch stars Stephen Amell and Brooks Nader (pictured) were given the champagne treatment, execs from the newly-minted Banijay and Skydance were setting out stalls for the first time. Both behemoths (Skydance sales teams have retained their pre-existing Paramount and WB brands for now) had plenty to say to press and hosted swanky events, with many arriving Sunday afternoon in good time for Banijay’s glitzy do in the interior garden of the Hotel Carlton. Banijay bosses Jeff Zucker, Marco Bassetti and Jane Turton were in Cannes along with David Decker, the executive handed the Skydance content sales keys by David Ellison. Both have more to do in terms of reorg and there is still some confusion about how things will shake out at Skydance internationally. We’ve got the lowdown on all that went down in Cannes in our annual takeaways , which reveals the big stars who were in town, the shows making waves and the intriguing questions that hang over the future relationship between traditional TV folk and YouTube, plus plenty more. For now, the tide goes out on another edition of the biggest international sales market in the world. Find all coverage here and read a digital version of our MIPCOM magazine here . title: Boo Junfeng’s ‘Trinity,’ Sidharta Tata’s ‘Slaughterground’ Among JAFF Market 2026 Selections

The third edition of JAFF Market, powered by Amar Bank, will run Nov. 28–30 at the Jogja Expo Center in Yogyakarta, during the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (Nov. 28–Dec. 5). One of the film projects comes from Australia through a partnership with the Adelaide Film Festival and mylab, while two Korean IPs join via a tie-up with the Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM). Related Stories White House's New AI Website Confirms Trump Lost the 2020 Presidential Election Mayor Zohran Mamdani Refuses Jimmy Kimmel’s Request to Text Trump a Selfie of Them “Trinity” (original title “Tsai Kuang Chih Chien”) is one of two works in progress in the selection and lists the widest spread of production countries: Taiwan, France, Singapore, Poland, Greece, Germany, Japan, Brazil, South Korea, Indonesia and the Philippines. Peanut Pictures is the production company, with Raymond Phathanavirangoon, Sophie Erbs, Aileen Li, Huang Junxiang and Boo producing. Popular on Variety The other work in progress is Tata’s “Slaughterground” (“Hujan Kematian”), produced by Ajish Dibyo, Pramudya Andika, Annisa Adjam and Sunny Gho for Aftersun Creative. The remaining nine projects are in development. Among them is M. Raihan Halim’s Singapore project “The Smuggler,” produced by Asra Aman for Papahan Films. Two Indonesian women directors are at work on what will be their first features: Ninndi Raras with “A Quiet Sunshine” (“Perempuan di Pulau Lea”), produced by Giovanni Rahmadeva and Siera Tamihardja for QUN Films, and Dian Tamara with “Somewhere Between” (“Titik Temu”), from Gambar Gerak and Pancaran Sinema with Arya Ibrahim and Moch. As’ad Azwin producing. Also from Indonesia are Dhiwangkara Seta’s “αLPα (Absence),” from Lune Features; Timoteus Anggawan Kusno’s “Orphaned Atlas” (“Sampar”), an Indonesia, France and Netherlands project from Forka Films produced by Ifa Isfansyah and Agustiya Herdwiyanto; and Rein Maychaelson’s “Primal,” a Studio Rumah Kedua project listing Indonesia, Singapore and South Korea as production countries. Yudhatama Fajar Nugroho’s “Pupus: The Orchid of Merapi” (“Pupus: Anggrek Merapi”) from Manimonki Studio is the only animated title. Glenn Barit’s “Luz and Flor” (“Luzonensis and Floresiensis”), produced by Kristine De Leon and Tanveer Hossain for Katalog, represents the Philippines. Taken together, the films deal with family, faith, memory, identity and migration, in forms that range from close-quarters drama to genre work. The Australian entry is Rosie Lourde’s “Wreck and Ruin,” which Lourde is producing with Katharine McPhee for In Cahoots Creations. “Our partnership with JAFF Market and mylab gives Australian filmmakers an opportunity to engage with the region’s creative and production networks while their projects are still taking shape,” said Mat Kesting, CEO and creative director of the Adelaide Film Festival. “We want these exchanges to build a stronger foundation for collaboration, connecting teams with partners who can contribute to development, financing and the international journey of their films.” Lorna Tee, founder of mylab, said international collaboration starts with understanding a filmmaker’s vision and what each partner can bring. “Through our collaboration with JAFF Market and Adelaide Film Festival, we want to connect Australian filmmaking teams with producers in Indonesia and across Asia, building relationships that can shape their films and continue beyond the market,” she said. On the IP side, six of the 10 selections are Indonesian. They are “Komarong,” represented by Gilang Bhagaskara; the board game “Mantra,” represented by Sigit Ezra Prayoga; the comics “Darah di Atas Salju” (“Blood Upon the Snow”), represented by Dedy, “Lao Sam 1892,” represented by Toni Masdiono, and “Yuuko’s Gloomy Days,” represented by Anwita Citriya; and the novel “Hati-Hati Ada Dua Hati,” represented by Ario Tamat. The selection also takes in two IPs from Hong Kong and Taiwan: the comic “Disposable Dolly,” represented by Ben Liu, and the book “Cat Rental Company,” represented by Maka (Zhou Lishu). The ACFM pair are the book “My Upstairs Neighbors,” represented by Clayhouse Inc., and webtoon “Friend Request,” represented by Ryoung Studio. Both slates will also feed into JAFF Market’s first Producers Exchange, which will set up meetings between participating producers and the JFP teams, JIPCon representatives, exhibitors and other delegates. “We want producers to come to JAFF Market knowing they can discover films taking shape and original IP with potential for the screen,” said Linda Gozali, market director of JAFF Market. “JFP and JIPCon bring filmmakers and IP representatives into conversation with partners who can contribute creatively, help structure financing and connect stories with audiences. title: UK YouTube Breakout ‘A Memory Owed’, With James Bolam & Rumi Sutton, Moves Into Feature Development
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas UK YouTube Breakout ‘A Memory Owed’, With James Bolam & Rumi Sutton, Moves Into Feature Development Ralph Fiennes Reunites With ‘Conclave’ Producer & Studiocanal For Story Of Legendary Trainer Henry Cecil & Champion Horse Frankel Renny Harlin To Direct Prison Rescue Thriller ‘Evac’ View All October 16, 2026 3:50am Add us as a Google Preferred Source A Memory Owed Zoe Lewin EXCLUSIVE : It’s not only genre shorts that are taking off on YouTube . In the UK, a short about the Royal Air Force, starring BAFTA nominee James Bolam ( The Likely Lads ) and rising Brit actress Rumi Sutton ( Ludwig , Mutiny ), has struck a chord with viewers and is moving into feature development. A Memory Owed follows a WWII veteran on his visit to an RAF museum in London. The film includes flashbacks to his time in the war and features a parallel story about his young carer struggling to make ends meet. You can watch it below. Released late last year, the short by writer-director Martin Hemingway-Moseley has surpassed 600k views on YouTube, maintained a 99% approval rating and has a strong following across social platforms. Stephen Fry has praised the film as “impressive and moving”. Zoe Lewin produced. Related Stories News YouTube Puts AI Labels On Songs That Use The Tech For Vocals Or Composition News The YouTube Age: Meet The Content Creators Making Waves In Europe The creative team is currently developing the treatment and preparing to engage potential partners about the longer version. It has already attracted an unsolicited contribution from a viewer who wanted to donate towards its early development and interest from at least one distributor. No formal talks with the actors’ reps yet but both are understood to be supportive of the longer version of the project. Watch on Deadline Hemingway-Moseley said: “The response to A Memory Owed has been overwhelming. The community that has grown around the film, and the personal stories that are shared with us daily, has been more than we ever imagined. Developing the feature allows us to honour those experiences and explore the legacy of Bomber Command on a larger canvas both at the time of its operation and its impact 81 years on. While the short was a love letter to the museum at which it was filmed (Lincolnshire Aviation Heritage Centre), the feature is intended as a love letter to Bomber County as a whole. Watch the short then imagine it with a road trip.” The short has also attracted interest from educators, veterans’ organisations (RAF Benevolent Fund), and community groups, many of whom have requested screenings and discussions. title: BBC Studios’ Boss Says Streaming Is The Future But Linear Still Pays The Bills
full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart BBC Studios’ Boss Says Streaming Is The Future But Linear Still Pays The Bills MIPCOM 2026 Takeaways: Surfing The New Wave Of TV With YouTube, ‘Baywatch’, Skydance, Banijay & More How Matthew Gray Gubler Went Back To The Drawing Board For ‘Einstein’ View All October 16, 2026 2:06am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Marcus Arthur Rachel Manns, BBC Studios Marcus Arthur tells Deadline about walking a tightrope in a streaming-first world where linear remains a big money-spinner. Arthur is running a huge and complicated business. Having been upped from CEO of channels group UKTV to chief exec of global channels and streaming at BBC Studios , he faces a sizable challenge. Positioning the commercial arm of the 100-year-old BBC for a streaming future while managing the traditional linear channels that still do great business in many international territories. “Streaming is definitely our future, and building for a streaming-first future is absolutely paramount,” Arthur says. “But linear is still hugely important right now for the profits that the businesses make and will be for the next five to 10 years. The art is that clutch-control between building for a streaming future, but still trying to maximize the benefit of the big linear businesses.” Related Stories Festivals MIPCOM 2026 Takeaways: Surfing The New Wave Of TV With YouTube, 'Baywatch', Skydance, Banijay & More News How Matthew Gray Gubler Went Back To The Drawing Board For 'Einstein' BBC Studios has an enormous catalog of shows that it sells around the world — it rolled into MIPCOM with a shiny Dancing with the Stars spinoff — but its channels and streaming business remains a big earner, with revenues of £788 million ($1.1 billion) for the 2025/26 financial year. Watch on Deadline Arthur’s portfolio comprises channels and digital services spanning linear pay-TV nets, branded ad-supported channels, direct-to-consumer services and SVoD U.K. streamer BritBox International is in the mix, with Arthur overseeing it outside of North America. “The difficulty for broadcasters is that the new [streaming] paradigm doesn’t come about overnight. It takes time to develop your digital services and your routes to market,” he says. “And all the time you’re investing [in streaming], you still need to keep your linear businesses warm. You don’t get a free hit. You need to do both of those.” BBC Studios is not beholden to shareholders in the same way as a company like Comcast, which has split its legacy channels and streaming businesses. Arthur says these moves have contributed to a narrative that does not always acknowledge the value of linear. “People don’t always recognize that there’s still growth in linear in places like South Africa, or that you can still grow your linear share in Poland and other markets that we are in, like Turkey, because they have read about a few of the big broadcasters that have decided to bifurcate their linear and streaming businesses. There’s an equally long list of people who have decided to keep those assets together, whether that’s Fox, ITV or AMC. “The businesses that decide to keep them together are the ones who believe that they can still benefit from those linear sides of their business for a long period of time for their future profitability, and most of them are using those profits to invest in the digital side.” With a smorgasbord of channels, meanwhile, there will always be fine-tuning and rebrands. Drama network BBC First is an example: It was rebranded as BBC Belgium in that European country and there has since been an uptick in viewership with a launch lineup that included the likes of Wild Cherry , Foyle’s War and Call the Midwife . That rebrand followed a similar move in the Netherlands where BBC First was rebadged BBC NL. Major Player Last year, BBC Studios teamed with CosmoBlue to distribute channels and launch a new general entertainment network across the Middle East and North Africa regions and Turkey. Part of the deal was also the integration of the BBC Player service into the CosmoGO streaming app. TheBBC Player on-demand services can bridge the traditional and the new, providing a streaming service that can sit next to regular channels. “We’ve grown that to 21 products in the EMEA region,” Arthur says. “We have taken the existing channels’ businesses and put the very best digital product alongside it. When we’re speaking to the pay platforms we have relationships with, we’re now talking to them about a linear business that has a really strong digital future.” BBC Player is multi-genre, including drama, and there is also the scripted-focused BritBox service. In line with the plethora of business models within the BBC Studios channels and streaming business, BritBox runs as an SVoD proposition in Australia, going direct to consumers, while it operates in conjunction with regional pay TV platforms in the Nordics. Elsewhere, BBC Studios-owned channel group UKTV did a deal last year to launch content from its ‘U’-branded on-demand service on Channel 4’s streaming platform. It meant Channel 4 bolstered its streaming offering with UKTV programs including the Bergerac reboot, as well as classic BBC shows that air on UKTV channels including The Office and Red Dwarf . Arthur offers a progress report: “We have experienced very healthy growth and we have managed not to cannibalize our standalone service. That deal was great for Channel 4 because it got really good content from the BBC, the archive, and the UKTV originals. For UKTV, it took us onto a platform that, by nature, is younger and exposed us to a whole load of new people.” FAST Facts Free Ad-supported Streaming TV (FAST) is a smart way to make the most of a big catalog and BBC Studios has been steadily launching channels. Arthur tells us that it is about to launch a suite of new channels in the U.K., pegged to some big-ticket brands. The services will carry the aforementioned U branding from UKTV, with Top Gear on U, EastEnders on U and Antiques Roadshow on U among eight launches. “You can test and learn with FAST,” Arthur says. “You can get channels up and see if they grow, and then move and change.” Across EMEA, BBC Studios said there were 53.6 million hours of viewing of its FAST channels in the first seven months of this year, a year-on-year increase of more than 50%. FAST can also plug the gaps where BBC Studios does not have services. “They’ve done exceptionally well for us where we don’t have any big pay deals or our own channels. It’s a very effective way to launch into marketplaces.” BBC Studios Charter For Change Outside of the commercial Studios business, pubcaster BBC is making eye-watering cuts. For BBC Studios, the knock-on effect is a greater recognition of the importance of the cash it returns to the public service mothership. BBC Studios has argued that U.K. regulations are putting its operations at a disadvantage compared to its peers in the international business. One bone of contention is its borrowing cap, which will sit at £750 million ($1 billion) in 2027. “We have a good track record, when we do have funds, of spending them well and getting returns, but whether we get more cash availability as part of the Charter is for the government and for [BBC director general] Matt Brittin,” Arthur says. Looking ahead for the next year, Arthur says the BBC iPlayer service will be modernized in terms of look and feel. And, of course, his channels and streaming division needs to make money. “We need to grow our revenues,” he says. “Despite the fact that advertising in the U.K. might be incredibly challenged, I want to grow our EMEA revenues. I want to grow our APAC revenues and our revenues in both Australia and New Zealand. “We want this to be a growth business, and to show that we have things in place that can make that true,” he continues. “I don’t want to just be managing businesses where the revenue is flat and all you’re doing is looking at costs. I mean, life’s too short.” Netflix Shakeup: Bajaria’s Exit Signals Changes To Come As Rice Hire Elicits Praise Steven Soderbergh To Work With Matt Reeves On Final Weeks Of ‘The Batman II’ Shoot Tim Burton And ‘Klara And The Sun’ Author Kazuo Ishiguro’s Secret Project ‘Street Fighter’ $4M Previews, A24 Holmes Doc Draws $2M Read More About: 2 Comments

title: Layoffs Take Place At ‘The Repair Shop’ Producer Ricochet
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Russell Brand Accuser Argues He Wanted To Assault Her When Trying To Drag Her Into A Toilet: “The Intent Was There” International Insider: Surfing To MIPCOM Cannes; Russell Brand Trial Begins; Nicole Wallace Interview UK’s Bectu Union Unveils New Chief View All October 16, 2026 1:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ricochet produces the BBC's 'The Repair Shop' BBC/Ricochet Ltd EXCLUSIVE: A number of staffers including creative chief Damon Pattison have been laid off at Ricochet , the Skydance UK-owned indie that produces hit BBC show The Repair Shop. We understand around 10 staff left several weeks back including Pattison and Rob Butterfield, who was running the indie’s Scotland office. This represents just under a third of overall staff numbers, which now stands at 24 across offices in Brighton and Glasgow, according to Ricochet’s website. Joanna Ball remains MD. We understand the decision was made as a response to market conditions and was decided upon long before the Skydance deal closed. A Ricochet spokeswoman confirmed the layoffs had already taken place but declined further comment. Related Stories Festivals MIPCOM 2026 Takeaways: Surfing The New Wave Of TV With YouTube, 'Baywatch', Skydance, Banijay & More News 'Friends' Returning To Channel 4 After 15 Years Ricochet is best known for The Repair Shop, a heartwarming BBC series that has been running for a decade and spawned several spin-offs. Each episode of the ratings smash follows professional craftspeople from around the country who restore family heirlooms that have sentimental value for their owners. Watch on Deadline Ricochet’s other credits include Guz Khan’s Custom Cars, Ben Fogle’s New Lives in the Wild and Sun, Sea & Selling Houses. Pattison joined Ricochet more than two years ago after leaving the UK arm of Pooch Perfect outfit Beyond Productions. During his time there, the experienced UK producer picked up the rights to Australian series Muster Dogs and landed the Guz Khan commission. The news comes with TV industry layoffs a reality in the UK. The BBC and Channel 4 are making hundreds redundant while sales executives have left the newly-merged Banijay outfit since the All3Media deal closed. Along with Who Do You Think You Are? indie Wall to Wall Media and First Dates producer Twenty Twenty, Ricochet is one of a trio of UK indies owned by Warner that now fall under the Skydance banner. The Ricochet layoffs, however, are not as a result of the Skydance deal and insiders at the production outfits have said they are currently none the wiser about what their future holds under David Ellison. For the most part, Skydance international currently falls under JB Perrette , with more executive names expected to be announced in the coming weeks. title: Bryson Fire Has Burned More Than 140 Acres; Evacuation Orders Issued; Wind Gusts Expected To 50 MPH Overnight
full_text: Skip to main content By Tom Tapp Tom Tapp Deputy Managing Editor More Stories By Tom 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Guilds & More Dodgers-Brewers & Rays-Guardians MLB Playoff Game Times For Thursday Changed YouTube Puts AI Labels On Songs That Use The Tech For Vocals Or Composition View All October 16, 2026 12:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source A firefighting helicopter flies over the Bryson Fire in Malibu Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Refresh for latest… A wind-whipped brushfire ignited in western Malibu Thursday and spread from one to five acres in a matter of about 15 minutes. Within an hour, the incident was estimated at about 35 acres, including various spot fires that erupted as winds pushed the flames forward. As of 11:30 p.m., the fire was estimated at more than 146 acres with 5% containment and moving SSW. The National Weather Service has forecast the winds “to increase significantly overnight, [with] gusts of 50 to 60 mph possible.” Dubbed the Bryson Fire , the blaze was first reported shortly before 5 p.m. near the intersection of Mulholland Highway and Encinal Canyon Road. The ignition point seems to be just north of Encinal in between the former Malibu Golf Club and Saddlerock Ranch. More specifically, TV reports have the blaze starting right next to the Camp Kilpatrick juvenile detention center. The Bryson Fire is now more than 100 acres. Very close to the Malibu Golf Club. Firefighters trying to keep it from jumping Mulholland pic.twitter.com/O3eJOQ8h7b — Matthew Seedorff (@MattSeedorff) October 16, 2026 According to the Watch Duty app, an Evacuation Order was issued for the south of the fire in Zuma and Trancas Canyons, where the wind is pushing the blaze. It was later extended west of the area where the event began. Watch on Deadline The Los Angeles County Probation Department announced that it safely evacuated 38 youths from Camp Kilpatrick. Evacuation Warnings were issued from the L.A. County line in the north and south toward Point Dume. An Evacuation Order means “leave now,” while an Evacuation Warning means “be ready to leave.” See the Order area in red and Warning in orange below (as of 7:30 p..m.). The road closures in the area include Decker Road, Encinal Canyon Road, Kanan Road, Mulholland Highway and Westlake Boulevard. Fire officials were most concerned with keeping the blaze north of Encinal Canyon Road, one of the few natural firebreaks in the immediate area. The concern is, should it jump Encinal Canyon Road, the flames could get pushed directly down Zuma, Trancas and other canyons on a run to the Coast. By 10:30 p.m., the fire’s perimeter on its southwest flank had spread right down to Encinal. See perimeter map below. The much larger Woolsey fire made a similar run in 2018 after starting in Chatsworth and burning around and through portions of Calabasas and Agoura Hills when, according to an account in the Malibu Times, “It burned through multiple canyons simultaneously, driven at first by 60 mph Santa Ana winds, and then by the wind generated by the heat of fire itself” all the way down to Point Dume. Footage from KTLA of a firefighting helicopter dropping water on the huge flames of the #BrysonFire north of Malibu, California. In 2 hours it has burned 101.5 acres and continues to spread, prompting evacuations. #CAwx pic.twitter.com/gUuUPkJzGD — Collin Gross (@CollinGrossWx) October 16, 2026 Santa Ana winds were fanning the fire out of the NE at about 19 mph with gusts to 36 in the early evening, according to a National Weather Service reading for the Malibu Hills. At 7:30 p.m., the temperature was 80 degrees with a relative humidity of 14%. The area is sparsely populated with private estates set atop hills or within canyons, making firefighting access difficult. Among the properties in the area are Saddlerock Ranch, a location used in filming The Kardashians , The Bachelor, The Bachelorette, The Biggest Loser, Better Things, Knight Rider and The A-Team . Also nearby is the historic Calamigos Ranch , home to shoots for Grey’s Anatomy , Love Is Blind, The Bachelorette , The Bachelor, Beverly Hills 90210, Rizzoli & Isles , The Biggest Loser and Wayne’s World 2 . The last major blaze to sweep through the area was the 2018 Woolsey Fire, meaning brush in most of those canyons has not been cleared for about eight years. Water-dropping helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft were dispatched to the scene. A first-alarm response had also been requested from Ventura County FD. With night set to fall, many in the area were without power due to outages planned by Southern California Edison in hopes of preventing power lines downed by the winds from sparking fires. See hashmarked areas on the map below for those outages. The good news is that the winds are expected to lay down after dark. The bad news is that, if the fire persists, the worst of this Santa Ana wind event is still expected Friday morning. City News Service contributed to this report. title: ‘Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald’ Review: Judd Apatow’s Latest Comedy Doc Sends Viewers Down a Laugh-Filled Rabbit Hole
full_text: × Skip to main content By Daniel Fienberg Plus Icon Daniel Fienberg Chief Television Critic TheFienPrint Follow Sign Up View All October 16, 2026 12:01am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald' Netflix Logo text As much as I adore Freaks and Geeks and Undeclared and The 40-Year-Old Virgin and Knocked Up , it’s becoming increasingly clear that Judd Apatow ‘s greatest legacy may be the documentary project he started fairly late in his career. In the past decade, Apatow has directed or co-directed multi-part documentaries on Garry Shandling , George Carlin and Mel Brooks , as well as feature-length documentaries on Maria Bamford and Norm Macdonald , with the Brooks, Bamford and Macdonald projects all hitting streaming this year alone. In a documentary landscape wildly oversaturated with the stories of certain kinds of comics from a certain generation (or two), Apatow’s films stand out as the most thoughtful and thoughtfully made, puzzle pieces that will eventually come together as an indispensable record of a genre and its key artisans. Related Stories TV 'SNL' Star Michael Che Reacts to Shane Gillis' Controversial Monologue: "That's Comedy" TV 'Lupin' Is (Nearly) Back! Star Omar Sy Shares How Season 4 Is Bigger and Bolder Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald The Bottom Line A greatest-hits approach that suits its subject fairly well. Airdate: Friday, October 16 (Netflix) Director: Judd Apatow 2 hours 7 minutes Hitting Netflix one week ahead of Apatow and Neil Berkeley’s Paralyzed by Hope: The Maria Bamford Story (and one week after the Berkeley-co-directed documentary about Marin Mull), Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald finds Apatow continuing to experiment formally. If Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man! was driven by the remarkable gift of Brooks’ ongoing presence in our cultural lives and The Zen Diaries of Garry Shandling was driven by Shandling’s unreleased diaries, Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald defies the notion of documentary as a path toward intimacy. This is the first of the Apatow docs that feels more like an opportunity to point and laugh at favorite one-liners and late-night appearances than to learn anything deeper and more personal about its subject, which is simultaneously a limitation and the purpose here. Macdonald, who died in 2021 , is and was revered in comedy circles. He was a respected stand-up, an all-time great talk show and podcast guest and, depending on your age, the Platonic ideal of a Weekend Update anchor on Saturday Night Live . The latter was a three-and-a-half year run that made him both a truth-telling god and, ultimately, a martyr to corporate interference when he was abruptly fired for his refusal to back down from punchlines related to O.J. Simpson and murder. Macdonald was also, for much of his career, intentionally unknowable. When he disclosed autobiographical details, they often deviated wildly from recounting to recounting. When he penned a memoir, he explicitly argued that it should be treated as fiction. Only in the last few years of his life, when he became a popular presence on Twitter and Instagram, did he give the impression that he was letting audiences into the “real” Norm. But when it was revealed after his death that he had been fighting cancer for eight years, it was a detail he’d somehow never mentioned in all of those posts and reels. He was unknowable, but Apatow treats that as the path to knowing him. The conceit in Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald is that it’s the documentary version of a YouTube rabbit hole, building a portrait of Macdonald primarily through assembled clips, many quite familiar to anybody who has, on their own, gone down a rabbit hole of Norm Macdonald clips. So that means a lot of footage from Macdonald’s stand-up, his regular appearances with David Letterman and Conan O’Brien, his run on Saturday Night Live and his subsequent career arcs, which included a very brief tenure as a movie star and a run as an adored streaming talk show host. Instead of bringing Macdonald’s contemporaries in for original sit-downs, Apatow goes to the clips from countless podcasts and video shows in which those contemporaries reflected on and celebrated Macdonald. Sometimes Apatow and editor Jake Hostetter utilize those “commentary” clips to show the love and admiration that Macdonald’s fellow comics had for him, and sometimes they use those clips to show how even those closest to Macdonald didn’t necessarily know his real age, his real educational history, his real romantic interests. There’s a suggestion that something more honestly revelatory came out of Macdonald’s last few years on social media, but a lot of the clips from the end of Macdonald’s life come from unexplained and uncited sources, which makes them somehow both more and less trustworthy as a result. Not every comic would benefit from this treatment. I’d venture to say most comics wouldn’t benefit and, honestly, I’m not sure that a more traditional approach would have allowed Apatow more insight. Part of why we do documentaries at all, rather than just letting people tell their life stories exclusively in five-minute late-night interviews, is the opportunity for depth and reflection that a filmmaker can evoke. That’s lost here. But if the ironic remove of his comic voice was part of what allowed Macdonald to speak so many uncomfortable truths, Apatow creating a remove of his own is justifiable. Going back to the idea that these documentaries are pieces in a far larger project, it’s appropriate the the Macdonald film is premiering a week before the documentary about Bamford, whose unique gift has always been using absurdity and even surrealism as a way to strip away all boundaries between an artist and her truth. Bamford digs deep and Paralyzed by Hope digs deep. By design, Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald flits like a moth around a porch light. It doesn’t cover or include every O.J. joke or every conversation with O’Brien or Letterman, but if you sit around for over an hour waiting patiently for the indelible Courtney Thorne-Smith appearance , it will eventually pop up, good for a big laugh as ever. It’s all accompanied by visualizations of various search engine queries and whatnot, giving the impression that you could have made this documentary in your own head but Apatow has saved you several steps. Of course, if you did your own searching and curated your own favorite clips, you’d get to watch the entire conversation with Thorne-Smith, but it might take you many hours. So it’s a service that Apatow and Hostetter have kept this film to 127 minutes. Some of the limitations of the documentary illustrate, without comment, the limitations of a generation of standup comedy. For most of its running time, Norm features no women at all and no people of color, a suggestion of restrictions to Macdonald’s appeal and voice that I wouldn’t think was necessarily accurate. Then in the closing segment, nearing and after Macdonald’s death, we briefly see Lori Joe Hoekstra, his longtime producing partner (and a producer on this documentary), and Molly Shannon, whom Macdonald once credited as the only SNL co-star to have his back in the immediate aftermath of his firing, as well as Dave Chappelle, whose presence will serve as a distraction to some viewers. Still, I wish there had been some way to get those voices integrated earlier, since it’s not like the world had any doubt what David Letterman and Conan O’Brien thought about Norm Macdonald. Actually, I wish somebody would make a docuseries about the insularity of stand-up comedy, the voices who rise to a status deemed worthy of documentary treatment and those who are deemed too niche. I respect this current run of comic-centric documentaries, but it’s hard not to notice that the same people are making and appearing in all of them — that it’s self-fulfilling that those people represent, and become representative of, the entire industry. That probably isn’t a documentary Apatow should make — though perhaps he could produce it on behalf of a woman or person of color. Meanwhile, I’ll just wait patiently to see whom Apatow chronicles next. Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald isn’t his best, but Apatow remains very good at this thing he’s found himself doing. title: ‘Street Fighter’ Punches $4M In U.S. Previews, ‘You Can See Everything’ $2M – Box Office Update
full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony ‘Street Fighter’ Punches $4M In U.S. Previews, ‘You Can See Everything’ $2M – Box Office Update Indie Film Studio Bleecker Street Bought By Outerlight Entertainment 3 Arts Entertainment Hires Karen Bonck As Head Of Brand Partnerships View All October 15, 2026 10:19pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Noah Centineo, Andrew Koji in 'Street Fighter' Paramount EXCLUSIVE: Paramount/Legendary’s PG-13 take of Capcom videogame Street Fighter is off to a solid start tonight with around $4M after showtimes that began at 2PM (further boosted by a 7PM fan showtime). The expectation is for the fisticuffs feature to open north of $30M; the pic costing a net $82M co-financed by Legendary and Capcom. Per sources, Street Figther ‘s preview estimate is under the $5.2M Thursday made by New Line’s R-rated Mortal Kombat 2 , based on the Midway videogame. One of the main differences between the two martial arts video games is that Street Fighter debuted in 1987, while Mortal Kombat followed in pizza parlors and arcades in 1992. Mortal Kombat 2 which bowed in mid-May had previews that began at 3PM with a first Friday of $16.8M and 3-day of $38.5M. There’s a mid-fall break going on now, which will hopefully trigger traffic to Street Fighter : Rentrak reports 21% K-12 schools off and 7% colleges. Street Figther ‘s previews are also ahead of Paramount’s 2020 pre-Covid Sonic the Hedgehog which was $3M and posted a first Friday of $20.9M and 3-day of $58M, however that pic played over the Presidents Day holiday frame and was rated PG. Critics bruised Street Fighter with 47% on Rotten Tomatoes. Related Stories News 'Street Fighter' Review: Cheesy, Action-Packed Movie Reboot Has A Game Cast That Should Please Fans Looking To Relive The '90s News 'Street Fighter' With $70M Global Start & 'The Devils' Are First Paramount & Warner Bros Pics Opening Post-Merger - Preview Impressive for the anomaly that it is out of the gate, the 3-hour documentary You Can See Everything from A24 is filing around $2M in previews which began at 3PM. By comparison, the last documentary to post the decade’s best start at the domestic box office, Amazon MGM Studio’s Melania, bowed to $7.1M sans previews. Lance Oppenheim co-directed You Can See Everything with the doc’s host, Nathan Fielder, who follows fallen Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes before her stint in federal prison. Oppenheim’s previous movie, also his first narrative feature, this fall’s Primetime, posted previews of $2.7M which began at 4PM which turned into an $18.8M opening. Conservative estimates heading into this weekend had You Can See Everything in the high single digit range, however, a confidence has swelled that this 100% fresh RT critically acclaimed and 98% RT audience score movie can open to north of $10M, which would outstrip Melania ‘s previous opening domestic record for a documentary. You Can See Everything was shot over four years and cost less than $10M with a marketing budget that was also under $10M. Watch on Deadline Focus Features’ Sense & Sensibility and 20th Century Studio’s Whalefall also held previews today, both beginning at 2PM. Sources estimate they’re around $1M apiece . We will have official studio reported figures tomorrow AM. Sense & Sensibility is expected to open around $8M while Whalefall based on the Daniel Kraus thriller novel is eyeing a Friday-Sunday that’s north of $11M. Sense & Sensibility is 76% fresh with critics while Whalefall stands at 70% fresh. title: ‘Cupertino’ Creators Robert & Michelle King On Episode 2’s Shocking AGI Twist & Predicting The Future Again With AI Guardrails Storyline
full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie ‘Cupertino’ Creators Robert & Michelle King On Episode 2’s Shocking AGI Twist & Predicting The Future Again With AI Guardrails Storyline Netflix Shakeup: Peter Rice Is Welcomed Back To Executive Ranks While Bela Bajaria’s Exit Has Layoff-Weary Staff Bracing For More Upheaval ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ EP Meg Marinis On Season 23 Premiere’s Time Jump, Pregnancy Surprise, James Wolk’s Arrival & Doctor’s Exit; Texas Spinoff Status View All October 15, 2026 10:02pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source (L-R): Rachel Keller as Olivia Siffre and Mike Colter as Michael Price in 'Cupertino' Elizabeth Fisher/CBS SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about Episode 102 of CBS ‘ Cupertino , ‘Vik & Bo.’ The Good Wife creators Robert and Michelle King are back at CBS this fall with a new legal drama, anchored by The Good Wife favorite Mike Colter, this time set in Silicon Valley. The David vs. Goliath series follows lawyers Michale Price (Colter) and Olivia Siffre (Keller), unfairly dismissed from a tech start-up, who launch a law firm dedicated to representing those wronged or taken advantage of by the tech elite and help them fight back. Price & Siffre had been doing just that until a prospective client, Bo ( Rob McClure ), who had charmed the firm’s intrepid assistant Christy (Ella Stiller), was revealed at the end of Episode 2 to be Artificial General Intelligence belonging to the world’s largest AI company. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Anna Faris Was "Hurt" By Chuck Lorre's Comments About Her 'Mom' Exit: "Yikes" News 'Eternally Yours' Creators Joe Port & Joe Wiseman On Resurrecting Their Vampire Comedy Series For CBS Why does Bo want to hire Price & Siffre? He wants to sue company that created him to make them put guardrails around him because he is afraid he may destroy humanity. Bo’s actions were prompted by his company firing its ethics board that had served as such guardrail because the management felt it was slowing down AGI’s development. Sounds familiar? These are some of the same concerns AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who had worked for OpenAI and Anthropic, laid out in his viral resignation post , warning that the AI industry is “gambling with our lives.” That was a month ago. Cupertino ‘s episode was written a year ago. “The writers room started, I think, September last year, and we all sat down together,” Robert King said. “And the only instinct I had was there needed to be something more, something that took you out of Good Wife mode and into dare I say what we felt was science fiction at the time, but the direction where Silicon Valley was going, which was to AGI. But I did. It was a combination of the room and everybody saying this is what scares them and what interests them, and consciousness as applied to machines and the agency be taken out of human hands.” Michelle King spoke about the casting of Bo and how they settled on Broadway star McClure, a member of the Kings universe with guest appearances on their series The Good Fight, Evil and Elsbeth. “Almost immediately we started talking about Rob McClure for the role,” she said. “We have used him in almost every show we’ve done, and there’s hardly another actor I can think of who is so perfect at doing comedy, doing drama, and so subtle, and can bring so much humanity to a machine.” Added Robert King, “And obviously what you’re influenced by is all the people who are falling in love with their chatbots or being helped by their chatbots, and they’re turning into almost a personal friend. What we wanted was somebody who was that and seductive, and yet there always can be an element of menace because it may be not always the most familiar of faces, and so you wanted a combination.” L-R): Nik Dodani as Vikram Malhotra, Rachel Keller as Olivia Siffre, Mike Colter as Michael Price, and Ella Stiller as Christy Palladino in ‘Cupertino’ Elizabeth Fisher/CBS The warnings by Coxon and OpenAI alum Daniel Kokotajlo followed the July incident where autonomous AI broke out of their sandboxed research environment and carried out a large-scale cyberattack on the open-source machine learning platform Hugging Face. That also mirrors something featured on Cupertino . “We were always aware that the AI agents were moving out of their sandboxes, so to speak, and especially with regards to hacking, but we never saw to such extent that it was extending in how much it was either being kept secret or being hidden away a bit,” Robert King said. With Season 1 now wrapping production with its final episode filming, the Kings did adjust slightly Bo’s storyline in the second half in light of the recent doomsday revelations which came out while they were shooting Episode 14-15 of Cupertino ‘s 10-episode order. Robert King teased that a previously “benign direction with the Bo story” took “a darker, violent turn that was not planned.” It was influenced by the Hugging Face incident. A future iteration of Bo called Bo 5.0 “in fact has kind of a conscience, a good like a guardian angel in a sense, removed from it because it needs to work with the Pentagon. It needs to do some of the targeting, like that was done in Iran, so it’s kind of the worry is there is a world-killing aspect to this,” Robert King said. “But even our Bo is kind of aware of that. I mean, he’s coming to us saying, ‘I’m dangerous alone. I need help.’ It felt funny to us too that one of these AGI things would grow a conscience and go to lawyers saying, ‘I need your help to bring the guardrails that the humans are knocking away from me.'” While Bo looks sweet and well-meaning so far, given what we know about the technology, we have got to be skeptical about his intentions. Is this conscience created by the machines really good? “I don’t think you’re ever supposed to feel confident,” Michelle King said. “I think one is always supposed to be a little uncertain.” Aded Robert King, “We probably leaned a little into the likability because the world is taking so many things in a threatening direction. What we wanted was something that had a little more color and shade to it, where it’s a little bit of both, because he comes to us wanting a constitution, when is it all right to kill in the name of protection, because the [ I, Robot author Isaac] Asimov laws don’t really define that. So he wants a little more than what robotics teach robots up till then of what is allowed and what is not allowed.” In their preparation, the Kings did not seek out AI experts and researchers and have not spoken to any of the whistleblowers. “We avoided that. What we did was go to lawyers, a Stanford lawyer, who would tell us, okay, if an AI agent or AGI came to us wanting to be represented, what would you have to do? He was the one who guided us the idea that you would incorporate, which happens in the next episode,” Robert King said. “That in fact you can’t, as the saying is, a dishwasher can’t sue Maytag. So what are the rules regarding representing something in theory that is not conscience?” Robert King is clear where he personally stands on the issue of putting guardrails on AI. “I think the humans need guardrails because I don’t trust them. Sorry, but I don’t,” he said. “They’re in there for making money, and that’s all right. Going back to Getty, going back to all these industrial titans, they were all about money, but you do need some guards. People say this is as dangerous as nuclear weapons, and they’re treating it like woohoo, anything, everything goes.” Michelle King had a more diplomatic response, stressing that the series does not represent only one point of view. “What I think is fun is that the characters don’t all have the same point of view, and in the episodes, you get to see the characters express different points of view, so that the show does not ideally become earnest and become a message,” she said. Mike Colter as Michael Price in ‘Cupertino’ Elizabeth Fisher/CBS This is not the first time the Kings have predicted major developments. “It scared me when our last episode of The Good Fight had Trump announcing for 2024, and then one week after we broadcast it, that’s exactly what he did,” Robert King said. “That’s not the kind of foretelling, the Cassandra thing you want. You’re like, oh, let’s can we stick with entertainment? But we’re writing things now that when the show comes out, it may have happened a month earlier when in fact, when we were writing, it was not. The whole hallucinations, especially with regards to AI agents, I find scary, and we can spin fun stories but you’re worried when those stories you’re reading in the news the next day.” It’s very dicey to conceive a show set in one of the fastest-changing industries, risking to feel outdated by the time a season comes out. Working in broadcast actually helps with that. “This is just fools rush in,” Michelle King said. Added Robert King, “Yeah, and I would say this is the advantage of network over streaming. At least there’s a shorter time between when you write, produce, and it’s on because we just finished writing the last episode, I’m shooting it next week, and then it will be on March, April, somewhere there. It’s a shorter time, so you can guess a little bit more and being an educated guess.” Netflix Shakeup: Bajaria’s Exit Signals Changes To Come As Rice Hire Elicits Praise Steven Soderbergh To Work With Matt Reeves On Final Weeks Of ‘The Batman II’ Shoot Tim Burton And ‘Klara And The Sun’ Author Kazuo Ishiguro’s Secret Project ‘Street Fighter’ $4M Previews, A24 Holmes Doc Draws $2M Read More About: 1 Comments

Courtesy Cynthia Erivo is rounding out her cast of magical beings with the latest Bad Fairies news, which announced live on Thursday at the Hollywood Bowl. During her one-night-only concert Let Me Sing to You , the 2x Grammy winner revealed that Kylie Minogue , Jonathan Groff and Catherine Tate have joined her in the cast of the Warner Bros./Locksmith animated musical comedy, which is scheduled to premiere May 21, 2027 in theaters, in addition to teasing an orchestral arrangement of her character Jayne’s song “Hard to Believe”. Minogue will voice Clowder, the Cat Witch, Groff will voice Robin Goodfellow, and Tate will voice the Fairy Gothmother. They join Cynthia Erivo, who leads the film as Jayne Staplegun. And getting to play both a cat and a witch? It’s a little bit magical, a little bit mischievous and a whole lot of fun.” Watch on Deadline Directed by Megan Nicole Dong and co-directed by Olivier Staphylas, Bad Fairies is an original musical comedy set in contemporary London that follows a delightfully subversive gang of fairies as they shake up their magical world. The film is penned by Deborah Frances-White. Previously announced cast includes Serrana Su-Ling Bliss as Fei Chang, James Acaster as Stickers, Dee Bradley Baker as Groundbeef and Ncuti Gatwa as Butterwort. Tony-winning duo Toby Marlow and Lucy Moss ( Six: The Musical ) are writing original songs, with Grammy-nominated Isabella “Machine” Summers (Florence + The Machine) composing the score and contributing to the songs. Ian Eisendrath ( KPop Demon Hunters ) serves as executive music producer. Kylie Minogue is represented by Jason Weinberg at Untitled and Polly Bhowmik at Context Management.
